speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT RESPECTING CONFERENCE HELD ON MARCH 9
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer very briefly to the federal-provincial conference. At the October meeting it was agreed that this conference would resume in committee at a time to be fixed by the Prime Minister after consultation with the premiers of the provinces. In reply to my letter of January last outlining the fiscal proposals put forward by the federal government, some of the provincial premiers did suggest another meeting.
In my letter of February 18, 1956, I said:
Since our federal responsibilities and commitments are now so heavy that we would not be warranted in making any increase in the basic offer we made in January, it may be that the provincial governments generally would not feel that there would be any advantage to be derived from another meeting to discuss fiscal relations.
The replies to my letter indicated, however, that a further meeting in committee was desired.
The conference resumed Friday morning, March 9, and adjourned at five o'clock that day. Although the meeting was, as had been agreed, in camera, it was agreed at the beginning that each delegation could make public any statement it wished to make during the meeting. Some of these statements have been made public and several provincial representatives have made additional comments to the press. I will not endeavour to add to what has appeared in the press, or comment on the substance of the matter before the budget debate. I should like, however, to table the statement made by the federal Minister of Finance at the conference and also a statistical table distributed to the provincial premiers which shows an estimate of how the federal proposals would operate in the fiscal year 1957-58. It should be noted that these figures are illustrative only and that they are based on an assumed increase of 5 per cent per annum over the 1955 levels in the yields of standard taxes and the insurance premium tax.
Perhaps hon. members would wish to have the statement of the Minister of Finance and
the statistical table printed as an appendix to Hansard, as was done with the other documents relating to this matter.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING REPORTED OUTBREAK IN SOUTHERN ONTARIO

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING REPORTED OUTBREAK IN SOUTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
In answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton), I should like to read the following memorandum with regard to rabies control:
Control measures followed in dealing with the present rabies outbreak in Ontario are (1) the isolation and quarantine of all suspicious domestic animals and of all animals which have been in contact with them; (2) in affected areas the strict application of control orders on dogs, with stray animals being impounded or destroyed; and (3) the operation of clinics for the free vaccination of dogs and cats where the incidence of the disease is considered to warrant it.
Every reported suspected case of rabies is immediately investigated by federal veterinary officers. The animal is isolated and, if rabies symptoms develop to the later stages, which is necessary for laboratory diagnosis, its head is sent to the department's laboratory. The veterinarians also quarantine for observation all animals known or suspected of having been in contact with the suspicious animal.
The tying up of all dogs in affected areas, and the disposal of strays, is an extremely important part of the control program. While such an order can be applied under the federal Animal Contagious Diseases Act, most
Inquiries of the Ministry municipalities also have dog ordinances which can serve the same purpose. In the present outbreak in Ontario this has been attended to adequately to date by local authorities.
Where rabies has occurred under circumstances which necessitate complete vaccination of all dogs and cats in the area as a control measure, vaccination clinics for that purpose are operated by the federal Department of Agriculture. Such clinics have been or are being operated widely in all districts of northern Ontario, in Renfrew, Victoria, Hastings and Northumberland counties and in an area around Galt and Guelph in Wentworth, Wellington, Waterloo and Brant counties. Approximately 51,000 dogs and cats have been vaccinated to date in those clinics. There is no charge for the vaccination of dogs or cats at those clinics but the government does not bear any part of the cost of having animals vaccinated privately apart from the clinics.
The present outbreak has centred very largely in northern Ontario which is, of course, the outcome of the fact that the primary focus of infection is in northern wildlife, and the northern areas are the most exposed to wildlife. One hundred and eleven cases were diagnosed in Ontario between April 1, 1955, and March 9, 1956, with 67, or well over half, being in wildlife. Eighty-six of those cases have been in the area north and west from Nipissing and Parry Sound. The next heaviest area of infection has been in that part of the province, which is also reasonably exposed to wildlife, bounded by Haliburton and Renfrew on the north, Hastings on the east and Victoria and Durham on the west. There have been 19 cases diagnosed in that general area.
Apart from central and northern Ontario, only six cases of rabies have been diagnosed in the province in the present outbreak, up to March 9. These consisted of one fox in Bruce county, two foxes in York county, one dog in Simcoe county on January 9, one dog near Galt on February 21 and a cat near Guelph on March 9.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to two questions put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs by the hon. member for Lambton West concerning the Welland canal. He asked:
Is the Welland canal kept open after navigation closes in the fall in order to take water from the great lakes?
The reply to that question is that, after the close of navigation, water is supplied through the canal for domestic use by adjacent municipalities, for process water by various commercial establishments and for power purposes, and is conducted through weirs and the canal channel but not through the locks.
The second question was:
If in the St. Lawrence seaway project the Welland canal is to be deepened, how much extra water would flow through the canal?

I intend on this occasion to devote my time to an outline of the position of the Canadian farmer. Other members of the Progressive Conservative party will direct their attention to the amendment which I intend to move and will fill in the necessary details. As far as I am concerned, I will merely outline the problem.
I think it will be agreed generally, for certainly it is the view of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the farm union organization of Canada and other farm organizations, that in every province the farmer today is caught in a ruthless and unrelenting squeeze between falling prices of farm products and rising costs of production. I am not in any way advancing an argument of depression when I say that the squeeze is of such a nature that, unless action is taken to meet it, it will, unless curbed, lead inevitably to bankruptcy of Canada's outstanding industry. That trend applies equally to the apple and the potato grower, the field crop producer, the dairy farmer, the livestock producer and the wheat farmer.
It is true that some protection against this trend has been afforded by the Agricultural Prices Support Act, but to too great an extent that act has been applied in piecemeal fashion and, indeed, in considerable measure has become a dead letter. There have been glaring inconsistencies in its administration. I need only mention one in connection with the maintenance of the floor on butter, and there is no objection taken to that. The government found itself in the position of having a surplus, which was not a surplus according to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and it committed what to many Canadians was an inexcusable act of policy. It purchased butter, it maintained the price, and then it sold a considerable portion of that butter to a communist country at a price some 21 cents less than Canadians were paying for butter. That, indeed, is regarded by many Canadians as an example of asininity in the government's ramshackle policy in the administration of the protection to which agricultural products are entitled under the act in question.
Take the question of hog prices. We have had this controversy over and over again in the past and yet, while the government denies that hogs are being purchased on the markets at less than the established floor prices, any member from the western provinces must inevitably, in the nature of things, have received letters including bills which indicate clearly that the floor is being breached and
Economic Position of Agriculture that farmers are not receiving the protection to which they are entitled. The fact is that the law lacks teeth to punish wrongdoers. Every farmer must become his own police officer; otherwise his rights cannot be preserved.
There is a constitutional division of powers which I am glad to learn will receive the attention of the Supreme Court of Canada during the coming summer. We hope that once and for all the delineation of powers between the federal and the provincial governments respecting the marketing of agricultural products will be determined.
I think it is only fair to mention that one or more provinces have done something in their own legislatures to protect farmers against a breach of floor prices. In my own province of Saskatchewan I should like to see the legislature, now in session, bring in legislation to preserve and, at least, aid in protecting the farmers, the hog producers, who find themselves today in a position of having to sell on a market in which the floor is being broken.
The squeeze which the farmer suffers results from the disparity in the relationship between the prices of farm products and the prices the farmer has to pay. When they are in proper relationship parity is established, and it is parity that the farm organizations across this country are asking for today. Not charity but parity. When one looks at the general price relationship one begins to realize how far in recent years that desirable end has been departed from. As far as parity is concerned, it must be related to a basic period which is regarded as one in which prices and costs are in approximate equivalence one to the other.
I know of no better definition of parity than that which appeared in yesterday's New York Times. I have made the necessary changes in the definition to meet the situation in this country. It is as follows:
Parity prices are the dollars and cents prices that give to farm products the same buying or purchasing power they had in a selected base period when prices received by and prices paid by farmers were regarded as in good balance. . . . It has been put this way: If you can sell a truckload of barley and buy with the money received so much food, clothing, building materials, fertilizer, farm machinery and other living and production items as you could in a chosen favourable period in the past then your barley is selling at a parity price.
It goes on to point out the difference between rigid price supports which have not proved successful and flexible price supports which have proved successful in the experience of the United States.
The farm problem today is one that affects the people of Canada as a whole. I think the

Economic Position of Agriculture best description of it is to be found in an editorial in the Ottawa Journal recently which had this to say:
It is everybody's problem in Canada.
Not only farm organizations have spoken of the need of action. Such organizations as the Canadian Congress of Labour and the chamber of commerce in Winnipeg have all pointed out the dangerous position in which Canadian agriculture finds itself today, affecting as it does the people as a whole. I think one of the finest briefs I have read has been that of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented to the Gordon commission. It sets out in detail the situation of agriculture and endeavours to project itself 25 years ahead and anticipate the situation of agriculture at that time. It points out that there are 611,000 farmers in Canada today, that the average investment of a farmer is $15,500 and that between 1926 and 1954, if you allow the farmer interest of 3J per cent on the amount of his investment, the average return of a farmer has been only 30 per cent more than the amount of the hired man's wages. Taking 1948 as a base of 100, we find this:	Farm prices in
1955 were 97-8; retail prices 117-2; costs of distribution, 148. That covers nine Canadian farm products. What also took place was this. A larger share of the consumer's dollar goes to -the other elements of distribution than goes to the farmer. When the period began in 1948 the share of the farmer was 59-3 cents on every dollar. Today that share has fallen to 53 cents. That is the reason the Canadian farmer is disturbed. He is faced by the advancing shadow of diminishing returns that more and more obliterates his share of the national income. His share of the national income has gone down in the last six years to an alarming extent. If you take the parity price as a basis in 1951 and compare it with the parity price today, this is what you will find. In 1951 farm prices were 10 per cent over parity or 110; that is the ratio figure. In September, 1955, that relationship had fallen to 81. During the same period of time the costs of the things which the farmer has to buy had increased by approximately 2 per cent. That statement is not a partisan statement. It is a statement by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture based on an examination of statistics and given to the dominion-provincial agricultural conference in Ottawa in December, 1955. On the other hand, since 1951 Canadian consumer expenditure has increased substantially, while the farmer's receipts for the same food have shown a marked decline. That is shown in rather full degree and I am not going to quote at any 

length from the annual presentation to the cabinet by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture on February 14, 1956. When my friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) produces what I choose to call statistical prosperity by the figures which he advances, I point out that the summary of * the views of this agricultural body is to the following effect:
. . . the notable exception in this picture of record prosperity is that of the farmer and his family. We do not claim that Canadian agriculture is in a depression such as we have known in the past. We do say that the farming industry is not sharing in Canada's new high level of prosperity .	.	. From the point of view of prices, farm
products now show a price decline, taken as a whole, to about 20 per cent below a fair relationship level-whether this is calculated on the base period of 1925-29 used by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture or the more recent period of 1943-45.
Farmers from coast to coast feel keenly that on the average their returns have become badly out of balance with those of other major groups in the nation. It is important to emphasize purchasing power in this connection because the farmer's difficulties are to be found as much in high prices of the things he buys as in a decline in the number of dollars he receives.
The decline in the farmers' position has not come about as a result of poor crops and lagging farm productivity.
That too is the view expressed by the interprovincial farm union in the brief which they presented to the government on the 16th of the month. I am not going to quote these figures-they are fully set out in the brief- except to say this. Since 1951 the ratio of operating expenses to gross income in agriculture in Canada has gone up 23-38 per cent in 1951, 30-77 per cent in 1952, 41-6 per cent in 1953 and 52-2 per cent in 1954; and apparently the trend continued in 1955, although final statistics are not available. At the same time the decline in net farm income has proceeded downward 10 per cent, 21 per cent and finally 48 per cent in 1954. These figures indicate that year by year the ratio of the operating expenses on the farm is going up and a decline in net income is taking place. The situation is the same in agriculture as it is in any other business. You cannot go on paying more for the things you buy while getting less for the things you have to sell.
The same thing has happened with regard to cattle and hog prices. The details given here indicate a pronounced reduction throughout the period from 1951 to 1954 and the first half of 1955. Cattle, 1951, on the weighted average price per hundredweight at public stockyards were $28.22; in 1952, $20; in 1953, $15.36 and in 1954, $14.45. During the same time the price of grade A hogs went down from $33.30 a hundredweight until in 1955, in the second half of the year, it stood at $23.17.

That trend downward has not been slowed up in recent weeks. That is one of the major complaints among hog producers, namely the fact that the floor as it exists today does not protect.
The Financial Post recently, in a 20-page
supplement in the November 12 issue, published a summary of Canadian agricultural trends. In it there was an article by David L. McFarlane, Professor of Economics at Macdonald College. I am going to quote just a couple of paragraphs of his remarks. He says:
Cash farm income, $2,812 millions in 1951 slipped to $2,377 millions in 1954 as prices declined. But farm costs have remained essentially at 1951 levels. Thus net farm income has declined much more rapidly than the gross figure. Net income, $2,189 millions in 1951, fell to nearly half this level, $1,126 million, by 1954.
He does not give the 1955 figures but the increase was of such a nature as to result in no greatly increased medium of prosperity. Then he goes on to say this:
It is hard for city people-unless in the position of workers in farm machinery plants-to realize that agriculture is having serious economic troubles. Alongside of an industrial boom with payrolls and profits setting records, we find agriculture in the worst position since the early war years.
The real meaning of the news columns which recite the difficulties of grain producers, dairy farmers, potato and fruit growers is something approaching comparative farm depression.
He goes farther in that regard than do the other quotations to which I have made reference. I would quote further in that regard in support of my contention, Mr. Speaker, but since my time is limited I cannot refer in detail to the supporting evidence which in every case bears out the contention of the opposition that the agricultural situation has worsened, and that since 1951 there has been a shrinking of Canadian farm income by approximately 50 per cent. When we went out of power in 1935 we assumed the responsibility of a campaign, repeated over and over again, that when we were in power things were bad but without regard to any world conditions that existed then and without regard to the drought that destroyed production and at the same time destroyed income. Ever since then my hon. friends to the right of you, sir, have posed as the exclusive possessors of the magic solution of all farm problems. They have been carried along by the prosperity that resulted from the war and, following the war, was continued in the postwar period in the cold war that was waged.
It is true, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was able to say to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) in
Economic Position of Agriculture regard to the contract with Hungary, that the wheat board is getting rid of a large amount of wheat.

I am glad my hon. friend interrupted because I think he will agree that Providence, not the government of Canada, brought about the disasters of flood and frost. The parity situation has been very thoroughly canvassed during recent years. We, in the Progressive Conservative party, tried to get some action on this matter on several occasions, but without success. One of the earliest occasions was in 1941, during the war. The last occasion when we moved an amendment regarding this question of parity prices was on March 23, 1953. At that time we pointed out a situation which was rapidly accelerating, namely the expansion of the spread. Our attitude was ridiculed. After moving the amendment on that occasion at page 3208, I used these words, which in the light of subsequent events were not far removed from the facts. I said this:
-I believe the demand on the part of Canadian farmers in general that action be taken now, before Canada finds itself in the position of having surplus production. We realize the needs of the NATO countries for all-out production in order to meet the eventuality that peace should cease to exist; and in order to maintain farmers on the farms something must be done to remove the squeeze that is taking place because of falling prices which have resulted, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, in a reduction in income of 12 per cent in 1952 over 1951, while the production of agricultural products was materially increased during the same period and farm costs have risen by 5 per cent.
At that time I moved this amendment:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to provide floor prices for agricultural products at such levels as to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship."
At that time we pointed out what was happening. What we pointed out then has been found, in the light of subsequent experience, to be correct. As far back as the national convention in October, 1948, we had enunciated our policy in this regard. I read that declaration in the light of subsequent events.
1. The Progressive Conservative party stands pledged to assure the maximum of stability of income to Canadian farmers. To this end we will enact permanent floor price legislation based on the following principles
(a)	A definite formula in the Farm Prices Support Act for arriving at floor prices.
(b)	The formula will allow for variations in production and demand for individual products.
(c)	Floor prices will be announced well in advance of the production period.

Economic Position of Agriculture
(d)	The floor price formula will be arrived at in consultation with representative producers.
We will establish a board of live stock commissioners similar to the board of grain commissioners.
We will give every legitimate encouragement to co-operative agencies whether relating to purchase, sale or credit.
We will extend the activities of the federal farm loan board so that farmers may take greater advantage of long term low interest rates in the purchase and development of their farms.
We will extend the facilities for agricultural research-
All these things, in the light of subsequent events, have been found to be actually needed to meet problems which have faced Canada since.

I intend to move, sir, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton):
That all the words after "That" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship."
Now, that is the amendment I intend to move, sir. On the basis of previous experience I would not expect that it would be regarded as other than an amendment that the government would not accept.
Today, in the world in which we live, we face one of the most all-embracing economic massive retaliation attacks by the U.S.S.R. that has ever been launched by any nation in all history. The U.S.S.R. failed in its cold war offensive. Now, it has launched an overall world economic offensive. It goes into a country that it has chosen as its victim and, with the promise of appeasing hunger at the moment, asks the people in reality to translate their hunger and their thirst into a reasonably higher standard of living than they have had in the past, and in return the people in those areas forfeit forever their freedom and their liberty.
In times like these I am one of those who believe that surpluses are not dangerous in themselves. I believe we have a responsibility to maintain a productive agricultural machine, and to assure to the farmer a fair and reasonable share of the national income, which he is not receiving today-and statistics prove it. The general attitude of farmers proves the truth of that statement. What we need is a national policy on agriculture.
There was a farm conference last fall, which representatives of the various provinces attended. That farm conference secured from the minister no general vista of the future of agriculture. No lead was given to producers in Canada, and no picture of the anticipated situation in agriculture. A simple declaration was made with respect to one or two matters. A floor was to be maintained. Except for that, there was not that leadership which the farmers of Canada, indeed the whole economy, have a right to expect. The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix said:
And it demonstrated that the federal government has no very clear idea (none that it will make public, at least) about what, if anything, it can do about the Canadian agricultural industry as a whole. Without worrying about the order of their importance, each of these points deserves consideration in some detail.
It asks for a lead. It says no lead was given at that conference, and goes on to say:
What the federal cabinet really will do remains anyone's guess.
Then, it goes on to deal with the difference in opinion as expressed regarding subsidies by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I suggest, therefore, that there is need for a declaration of policy on national agriculture. The last federal-provincial agricultural conference was disappointing. It achieved nothing except to bring a group together and advise them that something had been done, or would be continued, and then let them go home. It bore quite a similarity to the dominion-provincial conference of Friday last, when the provincial premiers came here and were told that nothing could be done for them except what they had already been told, and now they could go home. That is not the kind of leadership that Canadians deserve today. It is not the kind of leadership that will bring about that national unity that all of us hope for. A national conference on agriculture should be called. Representatives of the federal and provincial governments and of the farm organizations should work out a general policy for domestic and international trade. However, that conference should be delayed until such time as the supreme court

has finally determined the distribution of powers as between the federal and provincial governments.
Tomorrow we are to be visited by the peerless leader of the forces of democracy in NATO. Last summer some of us had the privilege of visiting NATO headquarters. General Gruenther, the spearhead of survival; has over and over again emphasized the need of unity among NATO nations. The president of Italy spoke to parliament a few days ago. What he emphasized above everything else was the absolute need of something being done to strengthen and maintain the NATO organization. Human nature being what it is, if threats of war and fears are removed, if cold war becomes warm smiles, the mortar that holds the NATO nations together is bound to become softened. We need to maintain the strength of NATO, to assure the preservation of the surpluses that are being built up as part of our joint defence. It is for that reason that we in the opposition believe that consideration should be given to the establishment of a food bank in NATO countries. The international food bank'under FAO has not proven possible because of the difficulties inherent in such a plan when nations both within and without NATO are members of that organization.
The soviet policy will challenge the free world. If the free world is to maintain its strength and be in a position to bargain from strength in the field of economics, the agricultural machine in our country must be maintained, and the Russians must not be permitted to have the initiative in the economic war.
We believe that one of the reasons for our situation is the fact that we have lost our markets. The British market for agricultural products is gone, to all intents and purposes. The total value of bacon shipped to Britain last year was about $3,600, compared with the tremendous shipments made during the days of the war and subsequently. Surely something can be done about that market. Denmark is getting out now. In September the Danish-British agreement will be terminated. Is this not the time to bring about once more aggressive action in this regard to secure those markets, or at least a portion of them? Is this not the time for the government to reconsider the convening of a British commonwealth trade conference to the end that we shall be able to disperse our farm products rather than concentrate them in the United States, which is close at hand and convenient? Our experience in the past shows us that that is dangerous to the preservation of our agricultural machine, because invariably when we have surpluses the United 67509-128
Economic Position of Agriculture States has surpluses, and the United States government has greater regard for the farmers of the middle west than it has for the continuance of the right of Canada to export agricultural products to that country.
What about Japan? Japan is a country that has always discharged its financial obligations. That country is a mighty market for agricultural products. It was suggested by a former member of this house, Milton Campbell, who now lives in Hamilton, that the market in Japan has a potential value greater than any other market anywhere in the world. Would it be too much to suggest that consideration be given to the advancement of assistance by way of loans so that Japan would be in a position to trade with us ana accept a considerably larger portion ot tne agricultural production of this country than is the case today?
Fourthly, I mentioned the economic offensive of the U.S.S.R. under which emphasis is being laid on seeking, through the stomachs of men in underdeveloped countries in Asia and Africa, to subvert their hearts. For several years we in the opposition have been contending that there is a dividend in advancing assistance to underdeveloped countries by way of agricultural products and the like by the extension of plans such as the Colombo plan. There were some who said we were idealists when we took that view, but what of the United States1 now? What of Britain and what of France? All three have declared that more and more we must alter our objectives in facing the new economic conflict from the U.S.S.R. and direct our attention to the contribution we make to assist those countries which have not the economic possibilities we have.
In addressing this house Sir Anthony Eden put it this way. He said that the free nations must, and I quote:
. . . raise the standards of living and provide economic help and confidence for peoples in underprivileged countries.
I believe that as part of our defence efforts there should be a diversion of some of our surpluses for the purpose of raising standards in underprivileged countries.
I come now to the question of the agricultural products act. The present legislation needs to be revamped. It needs to have teeth put into it. I mentioned the economic section in connection with hogs and the way in which the legislation is being evaded to the detriment of the farmer. The administration of this act has become loose and dilapidated. There is no means of enforcing whatever provisions may be passed by the board operating under that act. Should we not at this session amend the act to the end that it will become effective?

Economic Position of Agriculture
Next I mentioned in general the widespread disparity between the price the farmer receives and the price paid by the consumer. That disparity, that spread, deserves to be investigated. Many hon. members in this house want work to do. They would like to perform a worth-while work but have been denied the opportunity of making the contribution which their ability and training would permit. I would like to see the agricultural committee, when it is set up, undertake to make a preliminary investigation into those spreads. Then if after hearing evidence the agricultural committee finds it is circumscribed to such an extent as to be unable to come to a definite finding on the question which exercises the thinking of farmers all across the country today, I should like to see a royal commission appointed in order to investigate this spread and ensure a greater degree of equity to agriculture in assuring that the farmer would receive the largest possible percentage of the price ultimately paid by the consumer.
Finally, sir, I come to the need of making Canadian agriculture strong, effective and efficient. I have already mentioned that if the present price-cost relationship continues and the spread maintains its present rate of interest, the day is not far distant when the Canadian farmer will find himself in a situation dangerous to the future of agriculture in this country. That is not a partisan view. That is the view of the federation of agriculture, the farm union organization, and agricultural economists.
I have already mentioned that three years ago I had the honour of moving in this house an amendment based on what I then pointed out was a trend that was multiplying in its amplitude and would ultimately be most detrimental to agriculture. Amendments to that end had been moved previously. They were based on a declaration made by the hon. leader of this party in June of 1953 and also on the national policy of 1948.
In 1953 the hon. Leader of the Opposition said in effect, "We will appoint a national agricultural board for the purpose of establishing fair floor prices related to farm production costs."
At that time he and those associated with him endeavoured to place before the Canadian people the situation as they saw it. People did not accept the viewpoint that we then expressed. But looking back on the retrospect of events that have taken place since that time, we are able to say that if the stand we then took had been accepted in 1953, in the motion moved in March of that year, the Canadian farmer today would not find himself in his present position. In
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
the light of experience our views have proven to have been all too prophetically true.
The trend referred to in the amendment moved in 1953 has continued. Canadian agriculture today would not be in its present precarious position if action had been taken at that time on the basis of the experience of our neighbour to the south and also on the basis of the demands of farmers generally.
Therefore, sir, having already given notice of my intention to do so, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton):
That all the words after "That" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship".

Mr. Speaker, we in this group welcome the motion which has been placed before the house this afternoon. We are particularly pleased that the motion is drafted in such terms as to permit us to declare our support of the principle of parity prices. The support of the principle of parity prices is something which the members of this group and our party at large have supported from its very inception. It is part of our philosophy that governments should take whatever action is necessary in order to provide a measure of equality of treatment to all major sections of our economy. We do not agree and never have agreed with those who say that the role of government should be to keep out of the economy, to sit back as a referee and do nothing about falling incomes of various groups. We believe in government action and we certainly believe that government action is now needed.
I want to point out to hon. members of this house that the concept of parity prices is that the government shall so regulate the prices of farm products as to give to agriculture an income which bears a very direct relationship to the income of other groups in our economy. In the past the members of the Conservative party have always said that they have believed in a hands-off policy as far as the government is concerned, that they did not believe in regulation, that they believed in free enterprise, the freedom of prices to go up and down in the market. I am glad to see this apparent complete transformation that has now occurred and an indication that it is their opinion and philosophy that the role of government should be to set agricultural prices in a very direct relationship to the cost of production and to place that on a formula basis.

During this session there has been growing evidence that the Conservative party is learning, that their education is being improved. As the weeks go on they are coming more and more to agree with the stand which has been taken on various issues by the members of this group. We are very pleased at that and we welcome them because we believe that if the principle of parity prices is supported solidly by the three opposition parties it will definitely result in legislation, even from this government, which will bring about an improvement in the agricultural industry.

I know this is something the Conservative party would like to forget, I know it is something about which they have not been too proud. On May 17, 1954, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) moved this amendment:
That all the words after the word "That" to the end of the question be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to demonstrating its support of the principle of orderly marketing through livestock marketing boards by announcing floor prices with respect to cattle and hogs at levels not less than the average of the prices which prevailed during the period from January 1, 1951 to December 31, 1953".
It will be noted that not only did we present a motion which embodied the principle of parity prices; we spelled out the formula. Had that formula been adopted by the government it would have resulted in cattle prices being not less than $21 per hundredweight, and probably more than that with the increased cost of production. A debate followed that amendment during which some most interesting remarks were made by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness), a member of the Conservative party. The hon. member damned the motion in no uncertain terms when he said:
In my opinion this particular proposal comes very close to being complete nonsense, and I think bears no relationship to any realistic conception of what the livestock industry is, what conditions are or anything of that sort.
And then later:
For those reasons, perhaps, the formula is not a reasonable or realistic yardstick to use. The whole purpose of this resolution, if carried into effect, would be to socialize the livestock industry.
When we proposed a formula for livestock prices and demonstrated our support of livestock boards in May, 1954, the hon. member

Economic Position of Agriculture for Calgary North said that the motion was designed to socialize the agricultural industry. I am pleased that the members of the Conservative party are coming along and are now not only presenting a motion today but advancing the concept of full parity. As I am sure you would anticipate, Mr. Speaker, after the hon. member for Calgary North damned the resolution asking for a formula support price for cattle and hogs the Conservative party voted against a parity floor price for cattle and hogs. It was the policy of the Conservative party at that time, but I am glad that they have changed their policy now and are prepared to support a general system of parity prices.
There is a lot of opposition in the country to the concept of parity prices, and in the main the opposition is led by people who have parity prices for themselves. It is led by the big newspaper companies, it is led by Canada Packers, by Massey-Harris, by the big industrialists, by the great friends of the Conservative party and the great friends of the Liberal party. These people say it is wrong and foolish that the prices of agricultural products should be tied to the farmers' cost of production, but when they have anything to sell they, of course, not only tie their price to the cost of production but after having done that they add a very substantial sum to that formula and obtain for themselves very handsome profits.
When we advance the concept of parity prices all we are seeking to do is to give the farmer and agriculture something that is already enjoyed by every other major industry in the country, namely, that the products they have to sell will be related to the cost of producing those products. Certainly under the policy being followed at the present time there is no relationship between farm prices and the cost of production.
Even some consumers seem to feel that they have a stake in low prices for farm products, that if they can get prices to the farmer for agricultural products down the cost of food will come down, but that is very often not correct. It is quite possible, in fact, it often happens that when the farmer from time to time receives less and less for his product the consumer pays more and more for the same product. Therefore it is not amazing at all to find that from 1948 to 1953 the farmer's share of the consumer dollar was reduced from 59-3 to 53 and that from 1951 to 1955, when the index for farm product prices was dropping from approximately 116 to 98, a drop of 18 points, the drop in retail prices of food was only 3 points. The drop in the case of the producer was six times as great as the very small drop in retail food prices.
[Mr. Argue.l
I say it is possible to have adequate farm prices and reasonable costs to the consumer.
I believe that under the policies that have been followed we have not only allowed farm prices to fall to drastic levels but we have also created in the mind of the consumer the idea that if any savings are to be made they are to be made in shopping for food and that the thing to do is to get food prices as low as possible. How many consumers, how many men and women of this country are looking for bargains in food when they go out to buy. They expect to get cheap food. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) would like to see the floor price on butter reduced. He is one who would like to see lower food prices, bargain food prices, but the very same consumers who when they go shopping hope to get bedrock food prices think it is quite all right, quite in order, quite proper, to pay a very high price for a television set, a refrigerator or a new automobile. They do not go around shopping for bargains. They say that they want a good product, a quality product and they expect to pay a good price for a quality product.
I think it is wrong, I think it is ridiculous, for the government to allow food prices to fluctuate to such very low levels from the point of view of return to the farmer as they have been doing in recent times. All food commodities are going down. Under the policy being followed by the government the purchasing power of wheat is lower now than it has been in any ten-year period since 1891. The purchasing power of a bushel of wheat in 1953-54 was 70 cents. In the great depression from 1931 to 1940 the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat was 80 cents. The grain producer is losing out in the price-cost squeeze.
The results of these falling prices are very evident in the returns for farm cash income and farm net income. From 1951 to 1955- 1955 is an estimated figure-farm cash income fell from $2,811 million to $2,323 million. In the three year period from 1951 to 1954 farm net income fell from $2,154 million to $1,125 million, or a drop of 48 per cent in net income in a three year period. That is the result of the policy of the Liberal government. That is the result of the policy of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), a policy that over a three year period allows farm net income to fall by 48 per cent.

Does the government do anything about it? Nothing! Absolutely nothing! Has the farmer any reason to expect better treatment? I think he has. Although it has been quoted many times in the house,
I think it is well that I should quote again the statement made by the late prime minister, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, in a national radio broadcast on December 4, 1943, when he said:
If, to help the war effort, fanners are asked to accept a ceiling on prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to assure them against an agricultural depression after the war.

I should not say that the government did not make the gesture of keeping it, that they did not do a lot of window dressing. . . . the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions_

-and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.

The motion we have before the house calls on the government to adopt a system of parity prices for agricultural products, the basis of the policy of the government ever since December, 1943, when it was enunciated by the late prime minister. We say that today there should be no reason that the opposition would have to move this kind of an amendment. That has been the stated policy of the government. But it has forgotten about its own policy. It has turned its back on its own commitments. As far as the farmer is concerned, the government's policies have been a flop. The government has failed the farmer. It has failed the farmer in other ways in addition to failure to provide him

with a system of prices that will allow him to stay in business and make a profit. As a matter of fact, other agricultural legislation on the statute books has been allowed to deteriorate. The value of it has been allowed to wither away.
In 1939 we had the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The maximum payment at that time was $500, but the value of the payment has largely been cut in half because of the increased cost of production and the decreased purchasing power of the dollar. Prairie farm assistance which has been of great benefit to the farmers in time of crop failure is now only a partial benefit. It is only a shadow of what it once was. The Liberal government cannot say too often in this house and in other places that it believes in free enterprise, that it believes in private enterprise. The Liberal government does not believe in private enterprise at all. It believes in corporation enterprise, big business enterprise. In my opinion there are only two main groups in this country that are today engaged in private enterprise where the individual has an enterprise and where he is in competition with other individuals in the same enterprise. I refer, of course, to the over 600,000 farmers in this nation. One could name the farmers and the local storekeepers. They are the private enterprisers.
They are in a bad way under policies followed by this government which allow and encourage corporations to grow and gobble up the local merchants, and which allow only the huge farmer to make any kind of reasonable return, thus driving the farmers off the land. These policies are wrecking the farmers and making them go broke. These policies are making bankruptcy the way out for many local merchants in this country. So far as the local storekeeper is concerned, about all the government has ever done for them is to print in the Canada Gazette the fact that he has gone bankrupt; that is about all the attention the local merchant ever obtains from this government. This government does not believe in private enterprise at all. It believes in a policy which wrecks the only two large groups in our country today that are bona fide free enterprisers, namely the local merchant and the farmer. The policy of the government is to get rid of both occupational groups, in an economic sense, just as fast as it can.
The government's policy is not good at home and it is not good internationally. We have surpluses of agricultural products at home, and instead of worrying or complaining about these surpluses we should be glad we have food surpluses. We should be glad that in Canada today there are substantial
Economic Position of Agriculture reserves of food. We should be adopting a policy that will move that food to the people in Canada who need it and to the people in the world who need increased quantities. The other day the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) stated in this house that many people in his constituency were starving. He got the horse laugh from some people when he made that statement. I make the statement that it is a fact that in every single constituency in Canada, urban and rural, there are people who are starving. They may not be starving in the sense that they are hungry but they are starving in the sense that they are nutritionally starving. They can eat only certain kinds of food, not the protective foods. They cannot afford anything better. There are tens of thousands of old age pensioners, particularly in those provinces where there is no subsidy and particularly in areas where they have to pay large sums for room rent, who are nutritionally hungry. That being a fact, and with such huge surpluses of food as we have now available, butter, pork, milk, grain of all kinds, the government should undertake a plan to enable those people to purchase greater quantities of food.
I would suggest a food stamp plan. I would suggest a supplementary payment for the increased purchase of food for old age pensioners, blind pensioners and all of those persons who are receiving assistance in that way from the federal government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I may say we intend to support the amendment and the subamendment, because a policy of support prices for agriculture is absolutely essential in order that the industry be put in a position where it can operate on a sound basis.
I quite realize that a great deal has been said in this house during the past few years on the question of support prices. Unfortunately, in spite of the fact that a great deal has been said, very little has been done by the federal government in that regard. Until such time as the government does show greater attention to the need for support prices for agriculture that will make it possible for the farmers of this country to receive their fair share of the national income, discussions such as we are having today will continue.
It seems very strange to me that while the government shows very little attention to this question, on the other hand it recognizes the results of the situation. Instead of trying to cure the situation the government merely tries to take care of the result. By that I mean already this session they have brought down four bills making it possible for people to borrow more and more money. They recognize the fact that their policies today are driving the people farther and farther into debt. So, what do we have? We have had four bills already this session to make it possible for the people to borrow more money and go farther into debt. We have had the small loans bill, the farm loans board bill, the industrial bank bill and the bill to make loans available to farmers against wheat in storage.
As I say, apparently they recognize that their policies today are driving the people farther and farther into debt, and instead of trying to change the situation so that people do not have to go farther into debt, they merely open the doors to permit them to go still farther into debt which, Mr. Speaker, is not a solution. It can only lead this country into difficulties in the future.
The policy of support prices is criticized on two main counts. First of all, we hear it said, it is a hand-out; the farmers want another hand-out. The newspapers in eastern Canada and the financial institutions are very good at making that charge. Hardly a week passes that you do not find that charge made in some eastern paper. Strangely enough, I have never seen those papers criticize one

subsidy, namely that on gold, a direct handout, year after year, a hand-out far greater than the supports given to agriculture under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, leaving out the question of foot-and-mouth disease. If they are so much opposed to the idea of subsidies, why do these institutions not criticize the subsidy on gold? It all depends on whom the subsidy is for when they criticize it.
One hates to travel over ground that has been travelled over many times before in this house; nevertheless, so long as the present situation exists we shall continue to have to repeat things that have been said in former years, especially by farm organizations that come down here year after year and ask the federal government to take action.
What is the justification for support prices? I maintain the farmers of this country are not asking for a hand-out; they are not asking for anything to be given to them. They believe they have paid a premium on certain insurance, and now they expect the insurance to be made available. Let us go back to the 1930's, the depression years, when the prices of farm products were at a very low level. Anyone in this house who was farming in those years will remember what was said when the farm organizations appealed to the government for support prices on farm products. They were told no, this was an international situation. Prices had fallen in the world markets and the government could not do anything about it. The farmers could not expect to get more than world market prices.
That was the situation in the 1930's, and the farmers continued to get low prices. Then the war came along. Within a very few years after the declaration of war, farm prices went up. It might have been ppssible then for the farmers to recoup their losses and pay off some of the debt that had been accumulated in those years when wheat had been selling at 19 cents a bushel and other things at a similar level. The farmers were hoping that for a few years, anyway, they would get prices that would make it possible for them to pay off their debt's; but what happened? When prices went up in the world markets the government stepped into the picture and said, "World prices are too high. You cannot have world prices because we are going to put a ceiling on them." I maintain you cannot adopt the attitude that on the one hand when world prices are down the farmers have to take them, and on the other hand when world prices go up the farmers cannot have them. That has been the policy of this 67509-129
Economic Position of Agriculture government in the past, and that is largely the reason the farmers have suffered in the past. If it is fair to make the farmer take low prices when world prices are low, then it is only fair to let him have the high prices when world prices are high, and I shall quote some figures to prove that this has not been the case.
Apparently the government of the day realized there was some justification for what I am saying, because the prime minister of the day, Mr. Mackenzie King, as has already been mentioned, did state that in view of the government's policy the government would take steps to stabilize farm prices after the war, and the Agricultural Prices Support Act was enacted, which contains words to the effect that farm prices will be maintained at a fair relationship. Perhaps I should quote from the section of the act which deals with that question. Paragraph 9, subsection 2, reads:
In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection (1), the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
Mark this:
[DOT]-a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
Today the farmers represent around 16 per cent of the population, and they are getting 6-8 per cent of the national income, which shows that something has slipped very badly somewhere.
In my opinion the Agricultural Prices Support Act is a good act. The only trouble is that it is not wide enough; it does not provide support prices, apparently, for a sufficient number of agricultural products. For instance, it does not include grain. Quite a number of farm organizations have asked that grain be brought under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. As I say, it is a good act. I have no quarrel with the formula that was laid down, namely that the price of farm products today should be maintained at such a level that it will bear the same relationship to the price of other commodities as existed in the base years 1943, 1944 and 1945. That is the general basis for setting support prices.
When you take into consideration the fact that in 1943, 1944 and 1945 the prices of farm products were not high in relation to the prices of other commodities, I think the farmers are justified in expecting that under the Agricultural Prices Support Act farm prices today would be maintained at a parity with those three years. But what do we find? According to the agricultural prices

Econc.idc Position of Agriculture support board we find that the support price for butter is only 84-6 per cent of parity, of those base years; the support price of 23 cents on hogs is only 83 per cent of parity of that base, and the support price of 38 cents on eggs is only 56 per cent of parity of that base. That shows that the floor prices on the few products supported today are still quite a bit below the formula laid down by the government.
Wheat, of course, does not come under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. As I say, farm organizations have asked that grain should be brought under that act. It is interesting to note that if grain were brought under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, then the price of wheat, on the basis of the three years 1943, 1944 and 1945, according to the dominion bureau of statistics would be $2.27 a bushel.
Some people say, well, what would be the reaction of the public if the government maintained support prices at that level? For instance, what would be the attitude of labour? Well, I understand labour has already taken a stand supporting it. I refer to the brief of the interprovincial farm union council, presented to the government on February 16, 1956, and quote from page 13 in reference to this question:
That the consumer would not resist any move that would reimburse farmers on an equitable basis has been proven by the fact that the two main organized labour groups, C.T.L.C. and C.C.L., are on record as being in support of the principle of a fair and equitable price to the primary producer of agricultural products.
No doubt labour realizes it has a very substantial market in the farm industry, and if they hope to be able to sell to the farmers in large volume then the farmers will have to be able to pay for the goods they buy from the secondary industries. In order to do so the farmers will have to receive a price that bears a fair relationship to the prices on other commodities.
The wheat producer is, of course, in worse shape than the majority of farm producers because the price of grain has dropped lower than the price of any other farm commodity. Here again the grain farmers are fully justified in insisting upon an adequate support price today, in view of the fact that they did take a price considerably below the world market price in the years 1945 to 1949.
I have in my hand figures showing the losses that were suffered under the British wheat agreement by comparison with the world market price for class 2 wheat in the years 1946 to 1950, during which period the farmers lost $431,676,844. Then as the result of subsidizing the Canadian consumer at the same price at which we sold wheat to Britain

instead of at the world market price, the farmers lost another $136,920,921. If you add those two figures together you get an over-all total of $568,597,765. If you subtract from that figure $65 million which the government paid to the farmers on account of their losses, you have a net loss of approximately half a billion dollars.
Therefore I do not think any one can argue that the farmers in asking for a support price today are asking for a hand-out. They are merely asking compensation for something they have already paid. They have already paid the premium of half a billion dollars in regard to wheat and many hundreds of millions in regard to prices on other commodities.
I say this in view of the fact that they accepted prices considerably below the world market prices. There are several ways in which support prices may be paid or in which a parity price may be guaranteed. Personally I think the farmers are justified in asking for 100 per cent of parity with the period from 1943 to 1945 for all their produce whether it is sold in Canada or on the external market. On the other hand, however, we recognize that we have no control over the external market, though we do have control over the prices at which commodities are sold in this country.
We in this group have always advocated the adoption of the two-price system. It is interesting to note that the interprovincial farm union has also adopted this policy; that is, a parity price for the production of agricultural products consumed in Canada, and the best price that can be obtained on the world market, preferably through international agreement, for the farm produce sold abroad with a reasonable floor placed under the goods exported abroad.
After all, when you consider that approximately 94 per cent of all farm produce apart from wheat is consumed in Canada, there is no reason why we should allow the 6 per cent that is exported to set the price for the 94 per cent consumed in this country. Therefore we have advocated the two-price system, not because we do not think the farmers are justified in asking for a parity price on all their produce but because it is far easier to put a two-price system into operation. After we have had it in operation, then will be time enough to think about trying to obtain a parity price on the total production.
There are some people who will say that the adoption of a policy which will give the farmers of this country a price for their commodity that will return to them their fair share of the national income will expand the

amount of our surpluses. In that regard I think the time is long overdue for the government to announce a long-term policy. What is the government's policy regarding agricultural production? I think the government should announce to the farmers just what it wants them to do in regard to production. Does the government want the farmers to reduce their production or to maintain it at its present level? If the government wants them to maintain it at the present level, then no one can argue that a policy of price support is to blame for present levels of production, because if the government does not want production to be maintained at present levels it will have to adopt a policy whereby production can be restricted. But just so long as the government does not want production to be restricted there can be no criticism of the farmers' present level of production. When you consider the international situation wherein, according to the FAO, 50 per cent of the population is hungry, I think we can then agree that a policy of maintaining production at a high level is essential at this time.
We in this group have always stated in so far as external markets are concerned that we feel the government should make food available to all those nations who are unable to obtain it through normal channels of trade by such means as acceptance of foreign currency, by barter agreements or in some cases by way of gifts. In so far as the domestic market is concerned, we feel we still have quite a large potential market for increased agricultural production in this country.
The federation of agriculture in its brief suggested a number of means by which we could increase the consumption of dairy products. The federation suggested a free school lunch milk program, a continuation of the policy of making butter available to institutions, and some form of a stamp coupon program in order to get milk and butter to needy people. From time to time we have advocated a similar policy in this house. We have pointed out that a stamp coupon program could be adopted which would be similar to the stamp program carried out in the United States shortly before the war.
It is also interesting to note that the Canadian consumers' association, in a pamphlet they recently put out, also advocated a free school lunch milk program in order to expand the consumption of milk and an expansion of the program of converting milk into milk powder so it can be more easily stored.
If our surpluses continue to rise after the government has done everything conceivably possible to expand our markets for agricultural produce both in the domestic and external fields, I believe the government should 67509-129J
Economic Position of Agriculture then try to build up fairly substantial reserves of all farm commodities that can be stored against the day when crop failures might come. If when we have built up satisfactory reserves surpluses continue, I think the government would be justified in introducing a policy along the lines of the policy it adopted during the war, known as the wheat acreage reduction policy. I would say that policy would only be justified provided they had done everything in their power to expand the domestic and foreign markets and had built up substantial reserves to carry us over for two or three years of crop failures. They might set up something like the soil bank provided by President Eisenhower of the United States to encourage farmers to take poor land out of cultivation and put it into grass or forest. This would help to restore the fertility of the land; and if it were necessary to expand production later on, that land which had been sown to grass and was therefore in a more fertile state could be broken up and put into grain once again.
I submit that the government definitely owes it to the farmers of this country to announce just what they want in that regard. If they want the farmers to continue to expand their production, then they should guarantee that they will not have to suffer a lower price. If on the other hand the government feels that our production of agricultural products today is as high as it is wise to maintain it, the government should announce that and bring in a policy similar to that adopted in the United States in order to encourage farmers to preserve the fertility of their soil.

Mr. Speaker, in seconding the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert I should like to say first to the C.C.F. party to my left that this is definitely not a new policy on the part of the Progressive Conservative party. To prove this I go back to April 8, 1941, where I find on page 2280 of Hansard of that day an amendment moved by the then hon. member for Lake Centre, the present hon. member for Prince Albert, reading as follows:
That all the words after "that" in the motion be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor:
"it be resolved that the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agricultural and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture and in order that it may receive a just and fair return, and thus be enabled to make that contribution to Canada's war effort which is so desirable, and which our agricultural population so greatly desire to make."
That should make it plain to the C.C.F. party that this was first brought into the

Economic Position of Agriculture House of Commons by the hon. member for Prince Albert back in 1941.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-ECONOMIC POSITION OF INDUSTRY TRADE WHEAT    INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED SALES TO HUNGARY
speechtext: Would the hon. member go back to 1931?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-ECONOMIC POSITION OF INDUSTRY TRADE WHEAT    INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED SALES TO HUNGARY
speechtext:
I will go back to 1931 in a few minutes if my hon. friend will just wait. I should like now to quote from a speech made by a former leader of this party, John Bracken, at Lethbridge in 1943, when he said:
In order to prevent wide fluctuations of farm prices we shall, in the case of our major export products, provide a floor price below which they will not be permitted to fall, and we shall allow to the producers the benefit of any advance thereon. Since price ceilings are now being maintained to prevent farm prices from rising to high levels in wartime, we shall see to it that price floors are provided, to prevent farm prices from dropping to unfair levels in peacetime. There should not be price ceilings on farm prices to prevent inflation in wartime, without price floors to prevent deflation in peacetime.
Then on March 23, 1953, the hon. member for Prince Albert moved another motion, to be found at page 3208 of Hansard for that year, as follows:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to provide floor prices for agricultural products at such levels as to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship."
Surely that will answer the suggestion made by the hon. member for Assiniboia that this is a new policy on our part. It is not a new policy; we have stood for this policy for 15 years, and we are going to stick with it. As far as the C.C.F. subamendment is concerned we are quite willing to support it.
In regard to the criticism that we did not support the motion moved by the C.C.F. party on May 17, 1954, I think I should reread that motion, which is reported on page 4797 of Hansard and is as follows:
That all the words after the word "That" to the end of the question be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to demonstrating its support of the principle of orderly marketing through livestock marketing boards by announcing floor prices with respect to cattle and hogs at levels not less than the average of the prices which prevailed during the period from January 1, 1951 to December 31. 1953".
This party has never been in favour of a definite stated price for any particular period. We submit that it should be an elastic price. I think probably I should quote the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris to be found on page 4812 of Hansard for that same date. The hon. member said:
As a matter of fact, the present plan has been repudiated by the majority of livestock producer

groups in the province because it is too compulsory and, as has been indicated by the hon. member for Calgary North, it approximates socialized marketing. Among the groups who have not given their support to the plan are the Manitoba pools, which in a largely attended meeting in the city of Brandon just a few weeks ago, while supporting the broad principle of producer marketing boards, opposed to the extent of 90 per cent the proposal that has been put forward by the Manitoba farmers union. Also the Manitoba cattle producers association is opposed to the present plan.
I think we were quite justified in opposing that plan when it had been opposed by so many farm organizations across the country. The hon. member for Mackenzie suggested that I should go back to the 1930's, and I am ready to do that. I am willing to admit that when the Conservative government gave up power in 1935 the prices of agricultural products were low, but I would point out also that after five years of Liberal administration the inequality between the prices of the products the farmer had to buy and the prices of the products he had to sell had grown steadily worse.
In 1935, when the Liberals came into power, the parity prices were 20 per cent below; in 1940, after five years of Liberal administration, they had dropped to 23 per cent below parity. That should answer any question about the 1930's. I will say to the hon. member for Mackenzie that we are almost back now to the same ratio; we are closer to it than we have been at any time since 1932. I have here the Economic Annalist for February, 1956, volume 26, No. 1.
To prove the statement I have just made, I want to give farm prices of agricultural products from 1935 to 1940 on the basis of 100 for the 1935-39 price. In 1935 the figure was 88, in 1936 it was 96-9, in 1937 it was 119-7, in 1938 it was 105, in 1939 it was 91-8 and in 1940 it was 96-8. There was a rise of only 8-8 points in the period from 1935 to 1940. In the case of commodities and services used by farmers and taking the same period of years, 1935 to 1940, there was rise from 95-4 to 106-8, or an increase of 11-4 points. While farm prices fell 8-8 points the commodities the farmers were forced to buy rose 11-4 points.
Then we have the period from 1951 to the present time. On the same basis agricultural products have dropped from 296-8 in 1951 to a figure of 225 -05 for 1955, this figure being the average for the first eleven months of the year. That is a drop of 71-8 points. In the same period commodities and services used by the farmers have risen from 230 to 251-3, or an increase of 21-3 points.
I believe that gives a fairly good idea, Mr. Speaker, of the net position of the farmers of the country today, and after all it is the

net position that actually counts. The Minister of Agriculture can bring all the figures he likes on gross income and net worth statements, but the net income is the only one the farmer knows what it actually means as far as money in his pocket is concerned.
To go back again, I think most people from the west will remember the famous Gardiner dodgers that were used there in 1934 in the campaign prior to the election in 1935. 1 want to refer to what was on the dodger. It contained these words:
Dollar wheat will give you a job and enable you to own your own home. Dollar wheat will pay for your light and water and give you a telephone. Dollar wheat will pay your grocery bill and buy boots, shoes and clothing for the whole family.
