Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert, I do so for several reasons. No doubt many of those who have taken part in the debate thus far have, by contact with their constituencies and by reference to the dominion bureau of statistics and to speeches by other members, become aware of the plight in which agriculture finds itself today. I take part in this debate because of the fact that statistics show that farmers are receiving less and less of the total amount of money that is taken in by all the people in the economy, and that they are getting less and less of the national income, 19 per cent of the people receiving about 10 or 11 per cent of the national income.
They are also getting less and less of the consumer's dollar. Of every dollar the consumer pays for food, less and less finds its way back to the primary producer of that particular article, whether it be beef, bacon, strawberries or any other thing you want to mention. Net farm income has shown a steady decline over the past few years.
During this session the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture have explained to the Canadian people through parliament that the farmers are fairly well to do, and that over the years some thousands of millions of dollars have been taken in by the Canadian farmers.
These figures on income, of course, do not mean very much unless you know what are the costs. I do not propose tonight to discuss
Economic Position of Agriculture this from a high windy hill. I am going to take you down to the farm, just as I went to the farms last week end when I was home. I talked to some of the farmers there and I shall tell you what they are saying and what they are doing. When one reduces the subject to this basis, one finds out whether or not the farmers are making a lot of money and just what conditions are.
I find that there are more municipal taxes unpaid this year than for many years. I find also that those co-operatives serving farmers that do extend credit to their members have more unpaid bills and bigger bills than they have had for many years. I talked to these people last Saturday when I was home.
What has brought about these conditions? Not so many years ago we were warning the government that the loss of the British markets and the loss of other export markets would eventually be reflected in the Canadian economy. Such is the case, and it has now caught up with us. We listened to the debates on the wheat surplus in the Canadian west for about three weeks. We can look back and find that not so many years ago we were able to export over 600 million pounds of bacon and 147 million pounds of cheese to Britain in one year, as well as supply our own markets. Is it any wonder then that today, when we are barely supplying our home markets with these products, much less feed grain is being used by eastern farmers to finish livestock and produce cheese, bacon and many other products? This is having an effect not only on the income of the eastern farmers but on the western producer, because we are not buying such large quantities of coarse grains and low grade feed wheat for livestock purposes.
We are finding ourselves in this difficult position also because of inflation, as I have mentioned time and time again. We are living in a world where dollars are plentiful but they do not buy very much. We find ourselves in this position also, Mr. Speaker, because of the United States farm surplus disposal programs. In many cases the United States is usurping our traditional markets for surplus farm products.
While these events are taking place, there are a certain number of people who are more or less apologists for the policy or lack of policy, shall I say, of the government. I am just going to mention a couple of them. There is the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. We find the farmers' union coming into Ontario; and they are getting a foothold in Ontario because farmers believe the federation of agriculture has not been

Economic Position of Agriculture dynamic enough in supporting an agricultural program for this country. Then the president of the dairy farmers of Canada is saying, "Do not antagonize the government; be careful, and everything will turn out all right." That has been going on for quite a number of years.
Early in this session the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, "We are a party that believes in plenty; we believe in surpluses." Almost in the same breath he said there would be shortages of copper, shortages of steel, shortages of cement and many other things. The only thing of which he was proud was that there were surpluses of farm products. I can tell you that at the time Canadian farmers in southwestern Ontario were harvesting their onions, two carloads of onions were brought into this country from Egypt for no other purpose but to break the price.
I believe that is a rather shortsighted policy. We hear about surpluses in almost all farm products. This year there was supposed to have been a big crop of apples. As I go along the north shore of lake Ontario week after week I go through some of the best apple orchard areas in Ontario, and I am surprised at the number of orchards that have deteriorated in the past 10 years. I could say the same thing of my own county. I wonder sometimes if these surpluses are just fictitious, because when they are saying how many millions of bushels of apples may be produced as compared with five years ago or 10 years ago, they do not take into consideration that our population has been growing by leaps and bounds.
Take a look at the potato business. When we did have a crop of potatoes in this country there were 7,000 carloads of potatoes brought in from the United States; and the tariff is rather one-sided in favour of the United States. We have surpluses in many other products and will have when the products are imported like that.
I want to show you, if I can, just what is happening to those farmers to whom I was talking. I was talking to some of the concentrated milk producers, and they are not happy. Recently they have taken a cut of 10 cents per hundredweight in the price of their milk, from $2.65 to $2.55 per hundred for 3'5 milk. I was talking to one producer who last year produced 700,000 pounds of milk from over 100 cows on 300 acres of land. He is an efficient producer and has cost accounting facilities. He said that the milk cost him a little over $3 per hundred and it is now selling, as I say, at $2.55. At the same time powdered milk and cheese

are being imported from New Zealand so there will be dollars available with which New Zealand can buy Canadian manufactured products. This is sacrificing the agriculture industry to the manufacturing industry.
If anyone wonders why agriculture is sacrificed, I can tell him in a very few words. It is because for the last 20 years the government has booted around the agricultural industry; and then every four years when there has been an election, agriculture voted for the government. Agriculture is the only segment of our economy that can be treated that way and still support the government.
Coming back to the price of milk for a moment, I may say that in Ontario there is what is known as the dairy herd improvement plan. A survey of many of the dairy herds in the province was undertaken, and it was supervised by some of the experts from the college. This survey dealt with cost accounting and dairy farming. They found that the average cost of production for a large number of herds in the province of Ontario was $3.17 per 100 pounds of milk. Neither the cheese producers, the butter producers nor the concentrated milk producers were getting much over $2.50 for that very same milk.
Let us take a look at what the butter producer is actually getting. From 100 pounds of 3-5 milk an average of 4-2 pounds of butter will be produced, which sells at 58 cents a pound. That comes to $2.32. If the skim milk is manufactured into powder the skim milk powder is worth 11 cents a pound, which adds 88 cents to the $2.32. From that he must deduct the cost of manufacturing which he pays to his co-operative creamery, and that varies from 85 cents to $1.00. Therefore the farmer receives $2.30 for his 100 pounds of milk that costs him, according to all figures that can be produced, at least $3.00 or $3.17.
Another indication of the trend of the times is the fact that many young men who in the last five years purchased farms are finding it very difficult to meet their taxes and interest on their debt. In many instances the farm is deteriorating; in some instances they have given up, sold out and gone to town. That is not a healthy situation. I grant you that on the other hand there are many people who have bought farms and paid for them, but they have paid for them through the work of two or three people in their family besides their wives and themselves. They have paid for them because they have accepted a very low standard of living in order to pay for the home and the farm.

Let us take a look at the sheep industry. Recently the Minister of Agriculture made some announcement about a disease known as scrapie that has appeared recently in some of the flocks in this country. If they did not know of the seriousness of the disease, they should have known of it. Two years ago in Canada a certain flock was quarantined and none of the sheep could be exported to the United States. At the same time the breeder of those sheep was allowed to exhibit his flock at the royal winter fair. The Canadian people were told it was perfectly safe; it was a nervous disease, and they did not need to worry about it too much. That flock has been destroyed after its breeding stock has been scattered all over the country. I do not think there is one thing that has happened to the sheep industry in the last 100 years that could be as serious as this outbreak of scrapie which the government muffed and blundered through. It could ruin the export market for breeding stock as far as the sheep industry in Canada is concerned.
At very nearly the same time the production of wool in Canada reached an all-time low. This has happened to the sheep industry in Canada in the last few years. This careless attitude is indicative of the approach the government takes to farm problems. They do not require the Canadian manufacturers to indicate on their finished product whether the wool is shoddy, whether it has been used once or ten times over until it has lost all its life, or whether it is new wool that has just been clipped from the sheep. You can talk about grading. The wool is graded many times from the producer to the manufacturer, but once it reaches the manufacturer it is never graded again.
What about the cattleman? Last fall he could purchase cattle for 18 cents, 19 cents or 20 cents a pound. Today they are about 4 cents a pound less than they were last fall when he purchased them. After feeding them all the crops he grew on his farm he will not make too much money this year.
Take a look at the hog producer. I talked to some of them when I was home last week. Figures indicate that the over-all livestock population is increasing in this country. As far as the future markets are concerned, conditions indicate that there will still be a surplus. What about the hog producer? Many hog producers buy the young baby pigs when they are weaned, when they weigh an average of about 30 pounds. Let us say that the farmer who purchases them can buy them for $8. Some of them sold for as much as $12 or $15 last year, but let us say that the farmer could buy them for $8, which would be cheaper than if he raised them. He starts out with a pig that has cost him $8. If he buys all his 67509-130
Economic Position of Agriculture feed, which sometimes happens, he finds that it takes about 700 pounds of chop to finish a 30-pound weanling pig until it weighs 200 or 210 pounds. The total cost of the feed, plus the young pig, will run to at least $32.50. When he sells the hog it is sold on a dressed weight basis. A 210 pound hog will dress out at from 160 to 165 pounds. I looked over the purchases today, and I found that 161 pounds was the average dressed weight of that type of hog. If he sells it at the floor of 23 cents- I heard my friends to the left say that out west they are not getting that-it will bring him $37.03, or $4.53 per hog net. If my farmer back home wants to have an income of $2,817 next year he will have to feed and finish two hogs every working day of the year, 313 days. He will have to work 365 days. But that does not take care of taxes, interest on the investment or depreciation; and no pigs must die, not one. Therefore it does not look as if it is a very lucrative branch of the farming business.
If he should have his own grain and feed it his labour return per hog might be about $7, but that will not take care of interest, taxes or depreciation, and there will be no provision for' any extra labour that he might wish to hire. I took the trouble to call up the federal Department of Agriculture and to speak to one of their swine experts. I asked how much feed it took to finish a hog. He said, "It takes 400 pounds of feed for 100 pounds of gain". The 700 pounds I have given is 20 pounds less than the federal Department of Agriculture figure as the average for this country. If he had some pigs that were not thrifty, or if he was not too good a feeder, he would likely have a loss.
I venture to say that many of the farmers who are producing hogs are not making $4.53, or the $7 I have quoted, but probably more nearly $1 or $2.
Some say the farmers are not efficient. I have before me some figures taken from an exhibit sponsored by the Ontario department of agriculture at the 1954 royal agricultural winter fair. These figures point out that never in Canada's history has one hour's labour on the part of an urban Canadian purchased so much food. I will give you a few comparisons. In 1924 an hour's labour would buy 20 pounds of potatoes; in 1954 it would purchase 37 pounds, almost twice as much. In 1924 an hour's labour would purchase 1J dozen eggs; today it will purchase 2-6 dozen eggs, over twice as much. In 1924 an hour's labour would purchase 2-8 pounds of beef; today it will purchase 3-2 pounds. In 1924 an hour's labour would purchase 1-6 pounds of pork; today it will purchase 2 pounds. In 1924 an hour's labour would purchase 1-1 pound of butter; today it will

Economic Position of Agriculture purchase 2'5 pounds. In 1924 an hour's labour would purchase 3-8 quarts of milk; today it will purchase 7-3 quarts of milk.
I said something about farm efficiency. The number of farmers has decreased by 35 per cent over this period of 30 years, but at the same time the production by 35 per cent fewer farmers has increased by over 25 per cent in the years between 1935 and 1954 alone, to say nothing of the increase over the preceding years.
Farm production per man in Canada is up 70 per cent. I do not know how much more efficient the government or the Minister of Agriculture wants farmers to be, but I think-

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-ECONOMIC POSITION OF INDUSTRY TRADE WHEAT    INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED SALES TO HUNGARY
speechtext: I think they are probably the most efficient people in the country at this time.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-ECONOMIC POSITION OF INDUSTRY TRADE WHEAT    INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED SALES TO HUNGARY
speechtext:
I agree with you; in many respects they are. What reward are they getting for their efficiency? The more efficient they are and the more they produce, the less they receive. I sometimes wonder if it would not be a good idea for the farmers to sit back for about two weeks and not buy anything. We would see how soon people would begin to realize that the farmers' prosperity is also their prosperity.
I was going to refer to an article concerning the cost of producing hogs, but it was written at a time when pork was 28 cents a pound and it does not apply today very well. However, even when pork was 28 cents a pound, according to figures produced at that time by a butcher in the city of Toronto it was his claim that the farmers were making only $1 a hog and he was making a 23 per cent gain just by selling pork over the counter.
I did say something about onions being imported into this country. I wish to read from an article which appeared in the London Free Press on January 17, 1956. Mr. J. E. Reynolds, president of the Ontario fruit and vegetable growers' association, had this to say:
For instance, a boatload of Egyptian onions-
I believe I previously referred to a carload of onions. That was a mistake; I should have said a boatload.
-arrived in Montreal while the biggest crop of Ontario Sett onions in history was being harvested.
Other examples: 22 freight cars of potatoes were imported each day during June, July and August; 5,000,000 pounds of cabbage were imported in June, and 9,000,000 pounds of tomatoes entered the country during July, while local produce was left on the vines.
When we complain about this the government tells us it does not want to offend our neighbours to the south. There is a difference between being ignored by our neighbours to


the south and having them respect us. They will respect us more if we stand up for our rights instead of saying that we are afraid and we do not want to offend them.
In conclusion I wish to point out that a bill was passed in the legislature of the state of Maryland to prohibit foreign companies establishing themselves in Maryland. Our government say that protesting about such things as I have mentioned might hurt our good relations, but they are going to proceed to enact that bill all right; they do not care how much they offend us. The Lord looks after those who look after themselves, and I think it is about time we Canadian farmers and the government as representatives of the people began to do some of those things as well.
I am glad to support the resolution moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert and the amendment moved by the C.C.F. party.

Mr. Speaker, while New Brunswick is not one of the great agricultural areas of this country nevertheless it is an important industry in the province. In fact, considering its importance and some of the special aspects of it, I believe that the farmers of New Brunswick and of eastern Canada are more severely crushed by the price-cost squeeze than are those in other sections of the country. Quite a large proportion of the farmers in New Brunswick may be classified as mixed farmers, although a certain number, chiefly in my own constituency, might be classified as specialty farmers who specialize in potatoes. I might have something to say about potato farming before I conclude. [DOT]
Farming is an important subject to the province of New Brunswick; and while I am not a practical farmer, and it has been a long time since I had anything to do with practical farming, I must admit I was fairly well trained in it when I was young. According to the standards of farming at that time I do realize what farm work is like, and I am aware of the length of the working day and of some of the problems involved in farming.
It strikes me as strange when we are told that 1955 was one of the high spots in the prosperity of this country. We are told that in 1955 Canada produced more, exported more and consumed more goods and received more money than in any other year in our history, generally speaking. Nevertheless the farmers with whom I come in contact appear to be poorer, are having a more difficult time to pay their bills, and have less money in their pockets than they have had for a number of years. I can only speak

with some assurance of the people of my own constituency, and of course from what I read in reports about agriculture generally across the country.
Having listened to many speakers this afternoon who are practical farmers, and knowing what little I do about the situation in my own constituency and province, I am certainly in favour of the principle of this resolution. I feel that I would be remiss in my duty as a member if I did not stand up and more or less put myself on record as to the way I think farmers should be treated.
It seems to me there is only one conclusion one can come to in connection with the agricultural industry as a whole, and that is that the farmer is not getting a fair share of the consumer's dollar. That has been stated this afternoon in various ways, but regardless of how it is stated I believe that is what the farmer actually wants. He wants more of the consumer's dollar for the stuff he is producing. The spread between what the farmer gets for the products he raises, and which represent long hours of labour and large investment, and his costs is growing less and less. The percentages have been given and there is no need of my repeating them, but certainly the farmers' prosperity is not keeping up with the prosperity of other groups in the community, in the province or in the country.
Is there a solution? I listened to and read the speech of the right hon. Minister of Agriculture delivered on February 10 last. Apparently the minister had gone to great pains to work out a table of figures which he placed on the record. While there was no proof, there was certainly an inference in those figures that the farmers' cash and net income have increased for the last 20 years. I would not take issue with the minister on that. The minister is a most astute gentleman and clever speaker. He made a most significant statement toward the end of his speech. Having placed the table on the record, having reviewed the figures, he said words to this effect: Add all the facts together and you will get some idea whether the farmer is advancing or whether he is going backward in connection with his operations up to the present' time. That was for a period of some 20 years.
I reread that statement. It is a wide open statement. It is one in which you can read an expressed opinion. The right hon. minister has expressed the opinion, or has plainly left the inference, that the farmers of this country are far better off than they were 20 years ago, that they are a going concern, and that most of these complaints by farm and 67509-130i
Economic Position of Agriculture agricultural organizations are more or less unfounded, that they are a group of people who cannot be satisfied.
I am sure that if some city dweller, or someone who knew nothing of the farmer's problems, had been sitting in the gallery and had heard that speech, or had read it later, he would have got the feeling that the group of people engaged in agriculture in this country, farmers if you will, are possibly the best off people in Canada. I think they could honestly come to that conclusion after having studied that speech.
On the other hand, when you talk to farmers or to farm groups and hear them tell their story, you find that the picture is not so prosperous. It is a gloomy picture. At least 65 per cent of the people in my constituency are agriculturists, and the majority of the rest depends upon the farmers. Figures, statistics and net worth statements may not give a gloomy picture, but when I go out and talk to the farmer, when I look over his equipment, when I follow him from the time he starts out in the morning at five or six o'clock until he quits at night, I do not get that picture. As someone has said, the municipal authorities, the local merchants and the bankers do not give you that picture. You get a much gloomier picture than might be taken from the speech of the right hon. minister.
Toward the end of his speech the minister said in effect that the way any man found out how wealthy he was, whether he was better off than he used to be, is to put his hand in his pocket and find some money there. I should like the right hon. minister to go down to my constituency, talk to the farmers and find out how many of them have money in their pockets or can afford to go to town, take a trip or have a little pleasure. They have not the money to do it.
When you get right down to earth and go around the country and see buildings in need of repair, see vacant farms, see farms growing up in bush, see schoolhouses vacant, you get a much different picture. I was brought up in a country community. I went to a school where there were some 40 or 50 students, but today there are only 14 or 15 in that little school. A certain percentage are drained off at seven years of age to the central school, but the reason for the small number is that many of the farms which supported happy and fairly prosperous farmers in those days, people who were able to make a living, who were able to pay their bills, who lived as well as their neighbours did, have no one living on them today.
It was a friendly society. As a matter of fact, I still think a country community is

Economic Position of Agriculture one of the best places to live. The farmers are located within 50 or 60 rods of one another in a community extending for miles. Bui fee picture today has changed. You ask why has it changed? That is a fair question. I am not here to give the answer, but I can give my opinion based on what I hear. I do not believe that 6 per cent of the young men who have grown up within a radius of 20 miles of the home where I was raised have remained on the farms and carried on the family tradition. Why? Invariably the story is that they go and work at any other job.
Unfortunately they may leave New Brunswick, as a great many of them have done. They go to central Canada, western Canada or the United States and work at ordinary labour or go into business. It seems that almost anything is more attractive to them and more remunerative than farm life, although in my opinion it would have been a good thing for them to stick with the farm.
Many of the farms in my community that are still occupied are worked by older people, and time is running out on them. They are not working their farms very much. They are not able to do so any more. They cannot hire help to farm them, and their farms are deteriorating. It is a sad picture. Nevertheless I believe our people, if they can make as much money and have as good a life, are just as anxious to farm as the people of any other country. In a few cases people in my community have been fortunate, possibly in the potato industry. They were able to accumulate 300 or 400 acres of land, and if they were fortunate enough to have a few fairly good years there is the possibility that they can carry over a bad period. But in the last few years the bad periods have been coming so close together that even these people are beginning to come to the end of their rope, so to speak. The savings they were able to make are being used in order to carry on.
I do not think one needs. to labour this problem very much. I feel this way about it. If I were capable of giving the government advice there would not be much use of my doing so, because I think I would be wasting my time in imposing my ideas on the house and the Minister of Agriculture. If the government has not been convinced by those hon. members who have spoken today that something has to be done for agriculture; if the members of the government have not been convinced in their travels throughout the country, or if they are convinced that something should be done and do not know what


to do, then I think they should be prepared to accept some advice. I think they should give it a try.
Here is the other side of the picture. I believe it has been mentioned before, but I do not think I would be out of order in referring to it. In my constituency we have a very fine agricultural school. If there is any place in the whole province of New Brunswick where young people can be induced to go into farming it is in my constituency. Any young fellow who has any interest in cattle or stock of any kind, potatoes, mixed crops or grains of any kind has a grand opportunity to get a start. But our experience has been that a great many of these young men having taken two or three courses-the courses run through the winter -do not find it profitable to go back home and put into effect the ideas they have been taught. The smarter they are and the better farmers they would make, the greater the chance is that they will not stay in New Brunswick, and they do not even go to western Canada to take up agriculture.
In other words a fundamental industry, an industry which is very important to this country so far as the production of food is concerned, is losing a great many young men who I am sure would like to stay on the farms and improve our agricultural lands, who are the very persons who would improve the raising, grading and marketing of products because of their education. They are not staying on the farms. It is not that they do not want to but because it is not profitable for them to do so.
For that reason it seems to me that the resolution, if we think about it, does throw some light on the problem. The principle of the resolution indicates to our farmers that we consider they are entitled, in view of the number of hours they work and the risk they take in capital investment, to a fair return for their products and their labour. They are entitled at least to a square deal compared with people employed in other industries, whether in New Brunswick, any other part of the maritimes, or any other part of Canada. They are entitled to an equal deal with the people who are employed in other industries. I believe that legislation such as is envisaged by the amendment could be passed and that, properly administered, it could and would be of great benefit to the farmers.
On motion of Mr. Montgomery the debate was adjourned.

STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE march 9, 1956
At our October meeting the federal government put forward certain suggestions in broad outline. These were discussed quite fully at that time and later both in conversations and correspondence. They were then developed into definite proposals in the Prime Minister's letters of January 6 and February 18. We have circulated a statistical paper to indicate how these proposals would operate in the first year of the proposed arrangements, that is, in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1958. No one can foretell accurately either the level or the provincial distribution of population, incomes and profits one or two years hence, but we believe that the assumptions on which this table is based are reasonable.
Last October I suggested three principles or objectives that we ought to have in mind-
(a)	to assure as far as possible, to both the federal and provincial governments, access to revenues consistent with their responsibilities;
(b)	to develop and maintain fiscal arrangements that will contribute to high and stable levels of employment and that will tend to moderate rather than exaggerate the ups and downs in economic activity;
(c)	to promote simplicity, economy and equity in the tax system as a whole and in the machinery of tax collection.
The system of tax rental agreements, which is about to enter its tenth and final year, went a long way toward meeting these objectives, but experience has shown that it has not succeeded in meeting all the considerations to which the members of this conference attach importance. The proposals now before you are designed to reconcile as much as possible the various views represented around this table.
These proposals go just as far as we can go at this time in providing fiscal need grants and in reducing the extent to which we are occupying certain tax fields. On the assumptions we have made, our proposal will make available to the provincial governments $640 million in the first year of the new arrangements. This is $108 million or 20 per cent more than would be available to them if the present tax rental agreements were renewed 67509-131
and all the provinces took full advantage of them. The $640 million is made up of:-
(a)	Unconditional equalization grants	
$152 million(b)	Revenues from the personal income, corporation and succession duty fields, either by rental agreements or collection agreements, or by direct provincial imposition and collection without any extra burden on the taxpayer ..	465	"(c)	Removal of the tax oninsurance premiums from the definition of special corporation taxes

We believe that revenues of these magnitudes from these tax fields are consistent with the actual responsibilities at this time and what seems likely to develop in the next five years. Any province that considers that it requires larger (or smaller) revenues from these tax fields is, of course, entirely free to impose and collect whatever rates it deems proper; but if a provincial rate exceeds the standard rate it will not entitle the taxpayer to any additional credit or rebate from the federal treasury.
On our side, we cannot at this time make any further material concessions that would adversely affect our revenues. Defence expenditures have been stabilized in the past year or two at a high level (nearly $1,800,000,000). We can hope that they will not go higher, but we cannot be sure; neither is it wholly within our control, that they may not have to go up again quite sharply. Many of you will have noticed that defence estimates in both the United Kingdom and the United States have gone up this year.
During the past 15 years, with the consent, often at the urging of provincial governments, we have taken on very large new classes of expenditures in the field of social welfare- unemployment insurance, family allowances, old age pensions and assistance, and other measures-which this year are costing the federal treasury not far short of $900 million,

Dominion-Provincial Conference and are normally growing at a rate which will bring them over one billion dollars within five years. During the past year our total disbursement in these fields (including unemployment insurance benefits) was in fact over one billion dollars. All these payments have contributed to the maintenance of levels of incomes which have undoubtedly relieved the provincial governments of a great load of welfare claims that would otherwise have been pressed upon them and their municipalities. They have also had important beneficial effects on provincial revenues from all forms of taxation. They have been good and constructive expenditures, but their bearing upon the balance of revenues and responsibilities must not be overlooked.
Since we met last April the federal government has undertaken, subject to negotiated conditions, to assume costs in relation to unemployment assistance which in a year like 1954-55 would amount to about $25 million. We have also agreed in principle to assume additional costs of about $180 million a year in the field of health insurance. Now we are proposing arrangements which in the first year of operation and on the assumptions we have made will benefit provincial government treasuries by $108 million over and above the amounts already available to them under the tax rental agreement system. This, I assure you, is the practical limit of our capacity in these fields and at this time, having regard to all our other responsibilities, some of which, as in defence, are, in the last analysis, unlimited.
Our proposed stabilization payments are designed to give to the provincial governments an assurance of relative stability in these three tax fields. In effect we are offering every province unconditionally a guarantee that its annual revenues from equalization payments plus the yield or rental of the standard taxes will not fall below the higher of (a) its per capita rental available in 1956-57 multiplied by the current population, or (b) 90 per cent of its average actual revenues from equalization and stabilization payments and standard tax yields in the two preceding years. This is an offer of an unconditional floor in these tax fields, and a floor that keeps rising with our expanding economy. In the table before you, only Prince Edward Island and British Columbia benefit from this guaranteed minimum in 1957-58. We can all hope that the steady growth of our country is such that the floor will not often come into operation; but the insurance policy is none the less there.
The responsibility of promoting simplicity and economy in the whole field of taxation
belongs to all levels of government. As a federal contribution to this objective we are offering two alternatives-tax rental agreements and tax collection agreements.
We are prepared to offer each province a tax rental agreement covering all or any of these three tax fields for the five year period April 1, 1957 to March 31, 1962. The rental to be paid to the province will be the estimated total tax liability of taxpayers in that province at the standard rates of tax. The renting province need pass no taxing statute and will incur no administrative costs. It will, however, be bound for five years.
Alternatively, in the case of a provincial government having enacted and undertaken to maintain a taxing statute that in the opinion of the federal government does not differ from time to time in any material respect from the comparable federal statute and imposes the standard rates, the federal government is prepared to enter into an agreement to collect the tax for the provincial government. The federal government would remit periodically to the provincial government the amounts collected less a fee to cover the cost of collection. The fee we have in mind is 2 per cent of the amounts collected, providing the accounting procedures can be kept reasonably simple. A collection agreement would have to be for a period of, say, three years; or if for two years the fee would probably have to be 3 per cent. The cost of redesigning our collection machinery would not justify entering into agreements on a one-year basis. Notice to extend or terminate a collection agreement would have to be given not later than about the last day of April preceding the year to be affected.
While there seems to have been a general acceptance of the principle of equalization, there is, I realize, some conflict of views on the manner in which it has been applied. Some provinces with very substantial taxable capacity feel that their responsibilities are such that they should be accorded still more room in these tax fields. Other provinces, where taxable capacity is below the average, press for still larger equalization or fiscal need grants. The federal government is squeezed between these conflicting views.
If we were to raise the standard rates and lower the level up to which we equalize, we would find it impossible, except at a quite unacceptable cost to the federal treasury, to establish a formula which would not reduce the payments to most of the provinces to amounts below those available under the current rental agreements. It has been suggested that we should meet this by supplementary grants on a straight fiscal need basis.

While I would like to come as close to meeting all points of view as possible, I do not believe that experience with fiscal need payments, based on a sort of periodic means test, has been such as to encourage us to use them when the more objective approach that we have adopted is available to us.
Other ideas have been put forward and I assure you that they have all been given careful consideration. The co-operative use of these tax fields and the elimination of conditional grants have been suggested. The periodic collective determination of tax policies and an agreed division of the total yield does not seem to me to be a practicable policy. If there is any real support for this suggestion we would, of course, be prepared to study it after we have had some experience with our present proposals. As for conditional grants, it has been a tendency over the years for finance ministers and provincial treasurers to disapprove of them in principle, but
Dominion-Provincial Conference then- spending colleagues seem to keep pressing for new or expanded conditional grants.
Our proposals as now set out before you are an earnest effort to meet the differing and sometimes conflicting interests of the various provincial governments and at the same time maintain fully the strength of the federal government to meet its wide ranging and vital national responsibilities. Our proposals are not entirely new, but are, we think, a constructive adaptation of our past experience to our present problems. We have tried to meet adequately and sympathetically the needs of those provinces which have been having difficulty in providing standards of service which modern societies consider to be essential. But we have also had to keep in mind the preservation of the national interests of our peoples. The national interests and national security must be preserved if provincial autonomy is to have any real meaning.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer very briefly to the federal-provincial conference. At the October meeting it was agreed that this conference would resume in committee at a time to be fixed by the Prime Minister after consultation with the premiers of the provinces. In reply to my letter of January last outlining the fiscal proposals put forward by the federal government, some of the provincial premiers did suggest another meeting.
In my letter of February 18, 1956, I said:
Since our federal responsibilities and commitments are now so heavy that we would not be warranted in making any increase in the basic offer we made in January, it may be that the provincial governments generally would not feel that there would be any advantage to be derived from another meeting to discuss fiscal relations.
The replies to my letter indicated, however, that a further meeting in committee was desired.
The conference resumed Friday morning, March 9, and adjourned at five o'clock that day. Although the meeting was, as had been agreed, in camera, it was agreed at the beginning that each delegation could make public any statement it wished to make during the meeting. Some of these statements have been made public and several provincial representatives have made additional comments to the press. I will not endeavour to add to what has appeared in the press, or comment on the substance of the matter before the budget debate. subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING REPORTED OUTBREAK IN SOUTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
In answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton), I should like to read the following memorandum with regard to rabies control:
Control measures followed in dealing with the present rabies outbreak in Ontario are (1) the isolation and quarantine of all suspicious domestic animals and of all animals which have been in contact with them; (2) in affected areas the strict application of control orders on dogs, with stray animals being impounded or destroyed; and (3) the operation of clinics for the free vaccination of dogs and cats where the incidence of the disease is considered to warrant it.
Every reported suspected case of rabies is immediately investigated by federal veterinary officers. The animal is isolated and, if rabies symptoms develop to the later stages, which is necessary for laboratory diagnosis, its head is sent to the department's laboratory. The veterinarians also quarantine for observation all animals known or suspected of having been in contact with the suspicious animal.
The tying up of all dogs in affected areas, and the disposal of strays, is an extremely important part of the control program. While such an order can be applied under the federal Animal Contagious Diseases Act, most
Inquiries of the Ministry municipalities also have dog ordinances which can serve the same purpose. In the present outbreak in Ontario this has been attended to adequately to date by local authorities.
Where rabies has occurred under circumstances which necessitate complete vaccination of all dogs and cats in the area as a control measure, vaccination clinics for that purpose are operated by the federal Department of Agriculture. Such clinics have been or are being operated widely in all districts of northern Ontario, in Renfrew, Victoria, Hastings and Northumberland counties and in an area around Galt and Guelph in Wentworth, Wellington, Waterloo and Brant counties. Approximately 51,000 dogs and cats have been vaccinated to date in those clinics. There is no charge for the vaccination of dogs or cats at those clinics but the government does not bear any part of the cost of having animals vaccinated privately apart from the clinics.
The present outbreak has centred very largely in northern Ontario which is, of course, the outcome of the fact that the primary focus of infection is in northern wildlife, and the northern areas are the most exposed to wildlife. One hundred and eleven cases were diagnosed in Ontario between April 1, 1955, and March 9, 1956, with 67, or well over half, being in wildlife. Eighty-six of those cases have been in the area north and west from Nipissing and Parry Sound. The next heaviest area of infection has been in that part of the province, which is also reasonably exposed to wildlife, bounded by Haliburton and Renfrew on the north, Hastings on the east and Victoria and Durham on the west. There have been 19 cases diagnosed in that general area.
Apart from central and northern Ontario, only six cases of rabies have been diagnosed in the province in the present outbreak, up to March 9. These consisted of one fox in Bruce county, two foxes in York county, one dog in Simcoe county on January 9, one dog near Galt on February 21 and a cat near Guelph on March 9.

I intend on this occasion to devote my time to an outline of the position of the Canadian farmer. Other members of the Progressive Conservative party will direct their attention to the amendment which I intend to move and will fill in the necessary details. As far as I am concerned, I will merely outline the problem.
I think it will be agreed generally, for certainly it is the view of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the farm union organization of Canada and other farm organizations, that in every province the farmer today is caught in a ruthless and unrelenting squeeze between falling prices of farm products and rising costs of production. I am not in any way advancing an argument of depression when I say that the squeeze is of such a nature that, unless action is taken to meet it, it will, unless curbed, lead inevitably to bankruptcy of Canada's outstanding industry. That trend applies equally to the apple and the potato grower, the field crop producer, the dairy farmer, the livestock producer and the wheat farmer.
It is true that some protection against this trend has been afforded by the Agricultural Prices Support Act, but to too great an extent that act has been applied in piecemeal fashion and, indeed, in considerable measure has become a dead letter. There have been glaring inconsistencies in its administration. I need only mention one in connection with the maintenance of the floor on butter, and there is no objection taken to that. The government found itself in the position of having a surplus, which was not a surplus according to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and it committed what to many Canadians was an inexcusable act of policy. It purchased butter, it maintained the price, and then it sold a considerable portion of that butter to a communist country at a price some 21 cents less than Canadians were paying for butter. That, indeed, is regarded by many Canadians as an example of asininity in the government's ramshackle policy in the administration of the protection to which agricultural products are entitled under the act in question.
Take the question of hog prices. We have had this controversy over and over again in the past and yet, while the government denies that hogs are being purchased on the markets at less than the established floor prices, any member from the western provinces must inevitably, in the nature of things, have received letters including bills which indicate clearly that the floor is being breached and
Economic Position of Agriculture that farmers are not receiving the protection to which they are entitled. The fact is that the law lacks teeth to punish wrongdoers. Every farmer must become his own police officer; otherwise his rights cannot be preserved.
There is a constitutional division of powers which I am glad to learn will receive the attention of the Supreme Court of Canada during the coming summer. We hope that once and for all the delineation of powers between the federal and the provincial governments respecting the marketing of agricultural products will be determined.
I think it is only fair to mention that one or more provinces have done something in their own legislatures to protect farmers against a breach of floor prices. In my own province of Saskatchewan I should like to see the legislature, now in session, bring in legislation to preserve and, at least, aid in protecting the farmers, the hog producers, who find themselves today in a position of having to sell on a market in which the floor is being broken.
The squeeze which the farmer suffers results from the disparity in the relationship between the prices of farm products and the prices the farmer has to pay. When they are in proper relationship parity is established, and it is parity that the farm organizations across this country are asking for today. Not charity but parity. When one looks at the general price relationship one begins to realize how far in recent years that desirable end has been departed from. As far as parity is concerned, it must be related to a basic period which is regarded as one in which prices and costs are in approximate equivalence one to the other.
I know of no better definition of parity than that which appeared in yesterday's New York Times. I have made the necessary changes in the definition to meet the situation in this country. It is as follows:
Parity prices are the dollars and cents prices that give to farm products the same buying or purchasing power they had in a selected base period when prices received by and prices paid by farmers were regarded as in good balance. . . . It has been put this way: If you can sell a truckload of barley and buy with the money received so much food, clothing, building materials, fertilizer, farm machinery and other living and production items as you could in a chosen favourable period in the past then your barley is selling at a parity price.
It goes on to point out the difference between rigid price supports which have not proved successful and flexible price supports which have proved successful in the experience of the United States.
The farm problem today is one that affects the people of Canada as a whole. I think the

Economic Position of Agriculture best description of it is to be found in an editorial in the Ottawa Journal recently which had this to say:
It is everybody's problem in Canada.
Not only farm organizations have spoken of the need of action. Such organizations as the Canadian Congress of Labour and the chamber of commerce in Winnipeg have all pointed out the dangerous position in which Canadian agriculture finds itself today, affecting as it does the people as a whole. I think one of the finest briefs I have read has been that of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented to the Gordon commission. It sets out in detail the situation of agriculture and endeavours to project itself 25 years ahead and anticipate the situation of agriculture at that time. It points out that there are 611,000 farmers in Canada today, that the average investment of a farmer is $15,500 and that between 1926 and 1954, if you allow the farmer interest of 3J per cent on the amount of his investment, the average return of a farmer has been only 30 per cent more than the amount of the hired man's wages. Taking 1948 as a base of 100, we find this:	Farm prices in
1955 were 97-8; retail prices 117-2; costs of distribution, 148. That covers nine Canadian farm products. What also took place was this. A larger share of the consumer's dollar goes to -the other elements of distribution than goes to the farmer. When the period began in 1948 the share of the farmer was 59-3 cents on every dollar. Today that share has fallen to 53 cents. That is the reason the Canadian farmer is disturbed. He is faced by the advancing shadow of diminishing returns that more and more obliterates his share of the national income. His share of the national income has gone down in the last six years to an alarming extent. If you take the parity price as a basis in 1951 and compare it with the parity price today, this is what you will find. In 1951 farm prices were 10 per cent over parity or 110; that is the ratio figure. In September, 1955, that relationship had fallen to 81. During the same period of time the costs of the things which the farmer has to buy had increased by approximately 2 per cent. That statement is not a partisan statement. It is a statement by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture based on an examination of statistics and given to the dominion-provincial agricultural conference in Ottawa in December, 1955. On the other hand, since 1951 Canadian consumer expenditure has increased substantially, while the farmer's receipts for the same food have shown a marked decline. That is shown in rather full degree and I am not going to quote at any 

length from the annual presentation to the cabinet by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture on February 14, 1956. When my friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) produces what I choose to call statistical prosperity by the figures which he advances, I point out that the summary of * the views of this agricultural body is to the following effect:
. . . the notable exception in this picture of record prosperity is that of the farmer and his family. We do not claim that Canadian agriculture is in a depression such as we have known in the past. We do say that the farming industry is not sharing in Canada's new high level of prosperity .	.	. From the point of view of prices, farm
products now show a price decline, taken as a whole, to about 20 per cent below a fair relationship level-whether this is calculated on the base period of 1925-29 used by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture or the more recent period of 1943-45.
Farmers from coast to coast feel keenly that on the average their returns have become badly out of balance with those of other major groups in the nation. It is important to emphasize purchasing power in this connection because the farmer's difficulties are to be found as much in high prices of the things he buys as in a decline in the number of dollars he receives.
The decline in the farmers' position has not come about as a result of poor crops and lagging farm productivity.
That too is the view expressed by the interprovincial farm union in the brief which they presented to the government on the 16th of the month. I am not going to quote these figures-they are fully set out in the brief- except to say this. Since 1951 the ratio of operating expenses to gross income in agriculture in Canada has gone up 23-38 per cent in 1951, 30-77 per cent in 1952, 41-6 per cent in 1953 and 52-2 per cent in 1954; and apparently the trend continued in 1955, although final statistics are not available. At the same time the decline in net farm income has proceeded downward 10 per cent, 21 per cent and finally 48 per cent in 1954. These figures indicate that year by year the ratio of the operating expenses on the farm is going up and a decline in net income is taking place. The situation is the same in agriculture as it is in any other business. You cannot go on paying more for the things you buy while getting less for the things you have to sell.
The same thing has happened with regard to cattle and hog prices. The details given here indicate a pronounced reduction throughout the period from 1951 to 1954 and the first half of 1955. Cattle, 1951, on the weighted average price per hundredweight at public stockyards were $28.22; in 1952, $20; in 1953, $15.36 and in 1954, $14.45. During the same time the price of grade A hogs went down from $33.30 a hundredweight until in 1955, in the second half of the year, it stood at $23.17.

That trend downward has not been slowed up in recent weeks. That is one of the major complaints among hog producers, namely the fact that the floor as it exists today does not protect.
The Financial Post recently, in a 20-page
supplement in the November 12 issue, published a summary of Canadian agricultural trends. In it there was an article by David L. McFarlane, Professor of Economics at Macdonald College. I am going to quote just a couple of paragraphs of his remarks. He says:
Cash farm income, $2,812 millions in 1951 slipped to $2,377 millions in 1954 as prices declined. But farm costs have remained essentially at 1951 levels. Thus net farm income has declined much more rapidly than the gross figure. Net income, $2,189 millions in 1951, fell to nearly half this level, $1,126 million, by 1954.
He does not give the 1955 figures but the increase was of such a nature as to result in no greatly increased medium of prosperity. Then he goes on to say this:
It is hard for city people-unless in the position of workers in farm machinery plants-to realize that agriculture is having serious economic troubles. Alongside of an industrial boom with payrolls and profits setting records, we find agriculture in the worst position since the early war years.
The real meaning of the news columns which recite the difficulties of grain producers, dairy farmers, potato and fruit growers is something approaching comparative farm depression.
He goes farther in that regard than do the other quotations to which I have made reference. I would quote further in that regard in support of my contention, Mr. Speaker, but since my time is limited I cannot refer in detail to the supporting evidence which in every case bears out the contention of the opposition that the agricultural situation has worsened, and that since 1951 there has been a shrinking of Canadian farm income by approximately 50 per cent. When we went out of power in 1935 we assumed the responsibility of a campaign, repeated over and over again, that when we were in power things were bad but without regard to any world conditions that existed then and without regard to the drought that destroyed production and at the same time destroyed income. Ever since then my hon. friends to the right of you, sir, have posed as the exclusive possessors of the magic solution of all farm problems. They have been carried along by the prosperity that resulted from the war and, following the war, was continued in the postwar period in the cold war that was waged.
It is true, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was able to say to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) in
Economic Position of Agriculture regard to the contract with Hungary, that the wheat board is getting rid of a large amount of wheat.

I am glad my hon. friend interrupted because I think he will agree that Providence, not the government of Canada, brought about the disasters of flood and frost. The parity situation has been very thoroughly canvassed during recent years. We, in the Progressive Conservative party, tried to get some action on this matter on several occasions, but without success. One of the earliest occasions was in 1941, during the war. The last occasion when we moved an amendment regarding this question of parity prices was on March 23, 1953. At that time we pointed out a situation which was rapidly accelerating, namely the expansion of the spread. Our attitude was ridiculed. After moving the amendment on that occasion at page 3208, I used these words, which in the light of subsequent events were not far removed from the facts. I said this:
-I believe the demand on the part of Canadian farmers in general that action be taken now, before Canada finds itself in the position of having surplus production. We realize the needs of the NATO countries for all-out production in order to meet the eventuality that peace should cease to exist; and in order to maintain farmers on the farms something must be done to remove the squeeze that is taking place because of falling prices which have resulted, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, in a reduction in income of 12 per cent in 1952 over 1951, while the production of agricultural products was materially increased during the same period and farm costs have risen by 5 per cent.
At that time I moved this amendment:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to provide floor prices for agricultural products at such levels as to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship."
At that time we pointed out what was happening. What we pointed out then has been found, in the light of subsequent experience, to be correct. As far back as the national convention in October, 1948, we had enunciated our policy in this regard. I read that declaration in the light of subsequent events.
1. The Progressive Conservative party stands pledged to assure the maximum of stability of income to Canadian farmers. To this end we will enact permanent floor price legislation based on the following principles
(a)	A definite formula in the Farm Prices Support Act for arriving at floor prices.
(b)	The formula will allow for variations in production and demand for individual products.
(c)	Floor prices will be announced well in advance of the production period.

Economic Position of Agriculture
(d)	The floor price formula will be arrived at in consultation with representative producers.
We will establish a board of live stock commissioners similar to the board of grain commissioners.
We will give every legitimate encouragement to co-operative agencies whether relating to purchase, sale or credit.
We will extend the activities of the federal farm loan board so that farmers may take greater advantage of long term low interest rates in the purchase and development of their farms.
We will extend the facilities for agricultural research-
All these things, in the light of subsequent events, have been found to be actually needed to meet problems which have faced Canada since.

I intend to move, sir, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton):
That all the words after "That" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship."
Now, that is the amendment I intend to move, sir. On the basis of previous experience I would not expect that it would be regarded as other than an amendment that the government would not accept.
Today, in the world in which we live, we face one of the most all-embracing economic massive retaliation attacks by the U.S.S.R. that has ever been launched by any nation in all history. The U.S.S.R. failed in its cold war offensive. Now, it has launched an overall world economic offensive. It goes into a country that it has chosen as its victim and, with the promise of appeasing hunger at the moment, asks the people in reality to translate their hunger and their thirst into a reasonably higher standard of living than they have had in the past, and in return the people in those areas forfeit forever their freedom and their liberty.
In times like these I am one of those who believe that surpluses are not dangerous in themselves. I believe we have a responsibility to maintain a productive agricultural machine, and to assure to the farmer a fair and reasonable share of the national income, which he is not receiving today-and statistics prove it. The general attitude of farmers proves the truth of that statement. What we need is a national policy on agriculture.
There was a farm conference last fall, which representatives of the various provinces attended. That farm conference secured from the minister no general vista of the future of agriculture. No lead was given to producers in Canada, and no picture of the anticipated situation in agriculture. A simple declaration was made with respect to one or two matters. A floor was to be maintained. Except for that, there was not that leadership which the farmers of Canada, indeed the whole economy, have a right to expect. The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix said:
And it demonstrated that the federal government has no very clear idea (none that it will make public, at least) about what, if anything, it can do about the Canadian agricultural industry as a whole. Without worrying about the order of their importance, each of these points deserves consideration in some detail.
It asks for a lead. It says no lead was given at that conference, and goes on to say:
What the federal cabinet really will do remains anyone's guess.
Then, it goes on to deal with the difference in opinion as expressed regarding subsidies by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I suggest, therefore, that there is need for a declaration of policy on national agriculture. The last federal-provincial agricultural conference was disappointing. It achieved nothing except to bring a group together and advise them that something had been done, or would be continued, and then let them go home. It bore quite a similarity to the dominion-provincial conference of Friday last, when the provincial premiers came here and were told that nothing could be done for them except what they had already been told, and now they could go home. That is not the kind of leadership that Canadians deserve today. It is not the kind of leadership that will bring about that national unity that all of us hope for. A national conference on agriculture should be called. Representatives of the federal and provincial governments and of the farm organizations should work out a general policy for domestic and international trade. However, that conference should be delayed until such time as the supreme court

has finally determined the distribution of powers as between the federal and provincial governments.
Tomorrow we are to be visited by the peerless leader of the forces of democracy in NATO. Last summer some of us had the privilege of visiting NATO headquarters. General Gruenther, the spearhead of survival; has over and over again emphasized the need of unity among NATO nations. The president of Italy spoke to parliament a few days ago. What he emphasized above everything else was the absolute need of something being done to strengthen and maintain the NATO organization. Human nature being what it is, if threats of war and fears are removed, if cold war becomes warm smiles, the mortar that holds the NATO nations together is bound to become softened. We need to maintain the strength of NATO, to assure the preservation of the surpluses that are being built up as part of our joint defence. It is for that reason that we in the opposition believe that consideration should be given to the establishment of a food bank in NATO countries. The international food bank'under FAO has not proven possible because of the difficulties inherent in such a plan when nations both within and without NATO are members of that organization.
The soviet policy will challenge the free world. If the free world is to maintain its strength and be in a position to bargain from strength in the field of economics, the agricultural machine in our country must be maintained, and the Russians must not be permitted to have the initiative in the economic war.
We believe that one of the reasons for our situation is the fact that we have lost our markets. The British market for agricultural products is gone, to all intents and purposes. The total value of bacon shipped to Britain last year was about $3,600, compared with the tremendous shipments made during the days of the war and subsequently. Surely something can be done about that market. Denmark is getting out now. In September the Danish-British agreement will be terminated. Is this not the time to bring about once more aggressive action in this regard to secure those markets, or at least a portion of them? Is this not the time for the government to reconsider the convening of a British commonwealth trade conference to the end that we shall be able to disperse our farm products rather than concentrate them in the United States, which is close at hand and convenient? Our experience in the past shows us that that is dangerous to the preservation of our agricultural machine, because invariably when we have surpluses the United 67509-128
Economic Position of Agriculture States has surpluses, and the United States government has greater regard for the farmers of the middle west than it has for the continuance of the right of Canada to export agricultural products to that country.
What about Japan? Japan is a country that has always discharged its financial obligations. That country is a mighty market for agricultural products. It was suggested by a former member of this house, Milton Campbell, who now lives in Hamilton, that the market in Japan has a potential value greater than any other market anywhere in the world. Would it be too much to suggest that consideration be given to the advancement of assistance by way of loans so that Japan would be in a position to trade with us ana accept a considerably larger portion ot tne agricultural production of this country than is the case today?
Fourthly, I mentioned the economic offensive of the U.S.S.R. under which emphasis is being laid on seeking, through the stomachs of men in underdeveloped countries in Asia and Africa, to subvert their hearts. For several years we in the opposition have been contending that there is a dividend in advancing assistance to underdeveloped countries by way of agricultural products and the like by the extension of plans such as the Colombo plan. There were some who said we were idealists when we took that view, but what of the United States1 now? What of Britain and what of France? All three have declared that more and more we must alter our objectives in facing the new economic conflict from the U.S.S.R. and direct our attention to the contribution we make to assist those countries which have not the economic possibilities we have.
In addressing this house Sir Anthony Eden put it this way. He said that the free nations must, and I quote:
. . . raise the standards of living and provide economic help and confidence for peoples in underprivileged countries.
I believe that as part of our defence efforts there should be a diversion of some of our surpluses for the purpose of raising standards in underprivileged countries.
I come now to the question of the agricultural products act. The present legislation needs to be revamped. It needs to have teeth put into it. I mentioned the economic section in connection with hogs and the way in which the legislation is being evaded to the detriment of the farmer. The administration of this act has become loose and dilapidated. There is no means of enforcing whatever provisions may be passed by the board operating under that act. Should we not at this session amend the act to the end that it will become effective?

Economic Position of Agriculture
Next I mentioned in general the widespread disparity between the price the farmer receives and the price paid by the consumer. That disparity, that spread, deserves to be investigated. Many hon. members in this house want work to do. They would like to perform a worth-while work but have been denied the opportunity of making the contribution which their ability and training would permit. I would like to see the agricultural committee, when it is set up, undertake to make a preliminary investigation into those spreads. Then if after hearing evidence the agricultural committee finds it is circumscribed to such an extent as to be unable to come to a definite finding on the question which exercises the thinking of farmers all across the country today, I should like to see a royal commission appointed in order to investigate this spread and ensure a greater degree of equity to agriculture in assuring that the farmer would receive the largest possible percentage of the price ultimately paid by the consumer.
Finally, sir, I come to the need of making Canadian agriculture strong, effective and efficient. I have already mentioned that if the present price-cost relationship continues and the spread maintains its present rate of interest, the day is not far distant when the Canadian farmer will find himself in a situation dangerous to the future of agriculture in this country. That is not a partisan view. That is the view of the federation of agriculture, the farm union organization, and agricultural economists.
I have already mentioned that three years ago I had the honour of moving in this house an amendment based on what I then pointed out was a trend that was multiplying in its amplitude and would ultimately be most detrimental to agriculture. Amendments to that end had been moved previously. They were based on a declaration made by the hon. leader of this party in June of 1953 and also on the national policy of 1948.
In 1953 the hon. Leader of the Opposition said in effect, "We will appoint a national agricultural board for the purpose of establishing fair floor prices related to farm production costs."
At that time he and those associated with him endeavoured to place before the Canadian people the situation as they saw it. People did not accept the viewpoint that we then expressed. But looking back on the retrospect of events that have taken place since that time, we are able to say that if the stand we then took had been accepted in 1953, in the motion moved in March of that year, the Canadian farmer today would not find himself in his present position. In
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
the light of experience our views have proven to have been all too prophetically true.
The trend referred to in the amendment moved in 1953 has continued. Canadian agriculture today would not be in its present precarious position if action had been taken at that time on the basis of the experience of our neighbour to the south and also on the basis of the demands of farmers generally.
Therefore, sir, having already given notice of my intention to do so, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton):
That all the words after "That" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship".

Mr. Speaker, we in this group welcome the motion which has been placed before the house this afternoon. We are particularly pleased that the motion is drafted in such terms as to permit us to declare our support of the principle of parity prices. The support of the principle of parity prices is something which the members of this group and our party at large have supported from its very inception. It is part of our philosophy that governments should take whatever action is necessary in order to provide a measure of equality of treatment to all major sections of our economy. We do not agree and never have agreed with those who say that the role of government should be to keep out of the economy, to sit back as a referee and do nothing about falling incomes of various groups. We believe in government action and we certainly believe that government action is now needed.
I want to point out to hon. members of this house that the concept of parity prices is that the government shall so regulate the prices of farm products as to give to agriculture an income which bears a very direct relationship to the income of other groups in our economy. In the past the members of the Conservative party have always said that they have believed in a hands-off policy as far as the government is concerned, that they did not believe in regulation, that they believed in free enterprise, the freedom of prices to go up and down in the market. I am glad to see this apparent complete transformation that has now occurred and an indication that it is their opinion and philosophy that the role of government should be to set agricultural prices in a very direct relationship to the cost of production and to place that on a formula basis.

During this session there has been growing evidence that the Conservative party is learning, that their education is being improved. As the weeks go on they are coming more and more to agree with the stand which has been taken on various issues by the members of this group. We are very pleased at that and we welcome them because we believe that if the principle of parity prices is supported solidly by the three opposition parties it will definitely result in legislation, even from this government, which will bring about an improvement in the agricultural industry.
