I know this is something the Conservative party would like to forget, I know it is something about which they have not been too proud. On May 17, 1954, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) moved this amendment:
That all the words after the word "That" to the end of the question be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to demonstrating its support of the principle of orderly marketing through livestock marketing boards by announcing floor prices with respect to cattle and hogs at levels not less than the average of the prices which prevailed during the period from January 1, 1951 to December 31, 1953".
It will be noted that not only did we present a motion which embodied the principle of parity prices; we spelled out the formula. Had that formula been adopted by the government it would have resulted in cattle prices being not less than $21 per hundredweight, and probably more than that with the increased cost of production. A debate followed that amendment during which some most interesting remarks were made by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness), a member of the Conservative party. The hon. member damned the motion in no uncertain terms when he said:
In my opinion this particular proposal comes very close to being complete nonsense, and I think bears no relationship to any realistic conception of what the livestock industry is, what conditions are or anything of that sort.
And then later:
For those reasons, perhaps, the formula is not a reasonable or realistic yardstick to use. The whole purpose of this resolution, if carried into effect, would be to socialize the livestock industry.
When we proposed a formula for livestock prices and demonstrated our support of livestock boards in May, 1954, the hon. member

Economic Position of Agriculture for Calgary North said that the motion was designed to socialize the agricultural industry. I am pleased that the members of the Conservative party are coming along and are now not only presenting a motion today but advancing the concept of full parity. As I am sure you would anticipate, Mr. Speaker, after the hon. member for Calgary North damned the resolution asking for a formula support price for cattle and hogs the Conservative party voted against a parity floor price for cattle and hogs. It was the policy of the Conservative party at that time, but I am glad that they have changed their policy now and are prepared to support a general system of parity prices.
There is a lot of opposition in the country to the concept of parity prices, and in the main the opposition is led by people who have parity prices for themselves. It is led by the big newspaper companies, it is led by Canada Packers, by Massey-Harris, by the big industrialists, by the great friends of the Conservative party and the great friends of the Liberal party. These people say it is wrong and foolish that the prices of agricultural products should be tied to the farmers' cost of production, but when they have anything to sell they, of course, not only tie their price to the cost of production but after having done that they add a very substantial sum to that formula and obtain for themselves very handsome profits.
When we advance the concept of parity prices all we are seeking to do is to give the farmer and agriculture something that is already enjoyed by every other major industry in the country, namely, that the products they have to sell will be related to the cost of producing those products. Certainly under the policy being followed at the present time there is no relationship between farm prices and the cost of production.
Even some consumers seem to feel that they have a stake in low prices for farm products, that if they can get prices to the farmer for agricultural products down the cost of food will come down, but that is very often not correct. It is quite possible, in fact, it often happens that when the farmer from time to time receives less and less for his product the consumer pays more and more for the same product. Therefore it is not amazing at all to find that from 1948 to 1953 the farmer's share of the consumer dollar was reduced from 59-3 to 53 and that from 1951 to 1955, when the index for farm product prices was dropping from approximately 116 to 98, a drop of 18 points, the drop in retail prices of food was only 3 points. The drop in the case of the producer was six times as great as the very small drop in retail food prices.
[Mr. Argue.l
I say it is possible to have adequate farm prices and reasonable costs to the consumer.
I believe that under the policies that have been followed we have not only allowed farm prices to fall to drastic levels but we have also created in the mind of the consumer the idea that if any savings are to be made they are to be made in shopping for food and that the thing to do is to get food prices as low as possible. How many consumers, how many men and women of this country are looking for bargains in food when they go out to buy. They expect to get cheap food. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) would like to see the floor price on butter reduced. He is one who would like to see lower food prices, bargain food prices, but the very same consumers who when they go shopping hope to get bedrock food prices think it is quite all right, quite in order, quite proper, to pay a very high price for a television set, a refrigerator or a new automobile. They do not go around shopping for bargains. They say that they want a good product, a quality product and they expect to pay a good price for a quality product.
I think it is wrong, I think it is ridiculous, for the government to allow food prices to fluctuate to such very low levels from the point of view of return to the farmer as they have been doing in recent times. All food commodities are going down. Under the policy being followed by the government the purchasing power of wheat is lower now than it has been in any ten-year period since 1891. The purchasing power of a bushel of wheat in 1953-54 was 70 cents. In the great depression from 1931 to 1940 the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat was 80 cents. The grain producer is losing out in the price-cost squeeze.
The results of these falling prices are very evident in the returns for farm cash income and farm net income. From 1951 to 1955- 1955 is an estimated figure-farm cash income fell from $2,811 million to $2,323 million. In the three year period from 1951 to 1954 farm net income fell from $2,154 million to $1,125 million, or a drop of 48 per cent in net income in a three year period. That is the result of the policy of the Liberal government. That is the result of the policy of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), a policy that over a three year period allows farm net income to fall by 48 per cent.

600,000	farmers in this nation. One could name the farmers and the local storekeepers. They are the private enterprisers.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I may say we intend to support the amendment and the subamendment, because a policy of support prices for agriculture is absolutely essential in order that the industry be put in a position where it can operate on a sound basis.
I quite realize that a great deal has been said in this house during the past few years on the question of support prices. Unfortunately, in spite of the fact that a great deal has been said, very little has been done by the federal government in that regard. Until such time as the government does show greater attention to the need for support prices for agriculture that will make it possible for the farmers of this country to receive their fair share of the national income, discussions such as we are having today will continue.
It seems very strange to me that while the government shows very little attention to this question, on the other hand it recognizes the results of the situation. Instead of trying to cure the situation the government merely tries to take care of the result. By that I mean already this session they have brought down four bills making it possible for people to borrow more and more money. They recognize the fact that their policies today are driving the people farther and farther into debt. So, what do we have? We have had four bills already this session to make it possible for the people to borrow more money and go farther into debt. We have had the small loans bill, the farm loans board bill, the industrial bank bill and the bill to make loans available to farmers against wheat in storage.
As I say, apparently they recognize that their policies today are driving the people farther and farther into debt, and instead of trying to change the situation so that people do not have to go farther into debt, they merely open the doors to permit them to go still farther into debt which, Mr. Speaker, is not a solution. It can only lead this country into difficulties in the future.
The policy of support prices is criticized on two main counts. First of all, we hear it said, it is a hand-out; the farmers want another hand-out. The newspapers in eastern Canada and the financial institutions are very good at making that charge. Hardly a week passes that you do not find that charge made in some eastern paper. Strangely enough, I have never seen those papers criticize one

subsidy, namely that on gold, a direct handout, year after year, a hand-out far greater than the supports given to agriculture under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, leaving out the question of foot-and-mouth disease. If they are so much opposed to the idea of subsidies, why do these institutions not criticize the subsidy on gold? It all depends on whom the subsidy is for when they criticize it.
One hates to travel over ground that has been travelled over many times before in this house; nevertheless, so long as the present situation exists we shall continue to have to repeat things that have been said in former years, especially by farm organizations that come down here year after year and ask the federal government to take action.
What is the justification for support prices? I maintain the farmers of this country are not asking for a hand-out; they are not asking for anything to be given to them. They believe they have paid a premium on certain insurance, and now they expect the insurance to be made available. Let us go back to the 1930's, the depression years, when the prices of farm products were at a very low level. Anyone in this house who was farming in those years will remember what was said when the farm organizations appealed to the government for support prices on farm products. They were told no, this was an international situation. Prices had fallen in the world markets and the government could not do anything about it. The farmers could not expect to get more than world market prices.
That was the situation in the 1930's, and the farmers continued to get low prices. Then the war came along. Within a very few years after the declaration of war, farm prices went up. It might have been ppssible then for the farmers to recoup their losses and pay off some of the debt that had been accumulated in those years when wheat had been selling at 19 cents a bushel and other things at a similar level. The farmers were hoping that for a few years, anyway, they would get prices that would make it possible for them to pay off their debt's; but what happened? When prices went up in the world markets the government stepped into the picture and said, "World prices are too high. You cannot have world prices because we are going to put a ceiling on them." I maintain you cannot adopt the attitude that on the one hand when world prices are down the farmers have to take them, and on the other hand when world prices go up the farmers cannot have them. That has been the policy of this 67509-129
Economic Position of Agriculture government in the past, and that is largely the reason the farmers have suffered in the past. If it is fair to make the farmer take low prices when world prices are low, then it is only fair to let him have the high prices when world prices are high, and I shall quote some figures to prove that this has not been the case.
Apparently the government of the day realized there was some justification for what I am saying, because the prime minister of the day, Mr. Mackenzie King, as has already been mentioned, did state that in view of the government's policy the government would take steps to stabilize farm prices after the war, and the Agricultural Prices Support Act was enacted, which contains words to the effect that farm prices will be maintained at a fair relationship. Perhaps I should quote from the section of the act which deals with that question. Paragraph 9, subsection 2, reads:
In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection (1), the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
Mark this:
[DOT]-a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
Today the farmers represent around 16 per cent of the population, and they are getting 6-8 per cent of the national income, which shows that something has slipped very badly somewhere.
In my opinion the Agricultural Prices Support Act is a good act. The only trouble is that it is not wide enough; it does not provide support prices, apparently, for a sufficient number of agricultural products. For instance, it does not include grain. Quite a number of farm organizations have asked that grain be brought under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. As I say, it is a good act. I have no quarrel with the formula that was laid down, namely that the price of farm products today should be maintained at such a level that it will bear the same relationship to the price of other commodities as existed in the base years 1943, 1944 and 1945. That is the general basis for setting support prices.
When you take into consideration the fact that in 1943, 1944 and 1945 the prices of farm products were not high in relation to the prices of other commodities, I think the farmers are justified in expecting that under the Agricultural Prices Support Act farm prices today would be maintained at a parity with those three years. But what do we find? According to the agricultural prices

Econc.idc Position of Agriculture support board we find that the support price for butter is only 84-6 per cent of parity, of those base years; the support price of 23 cents on hogs is only 83 per cent of parity of that base, and the support price of 38 cents on eggs is only 56 per cent of parity of that base. That shows that the floor prices on the few products supported today are still quite a bit below the formula laid down by the government.
Wheat, of course, does not come under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. As I say, farm organizations have asked that grain should be brought under that act. It is interesting to note that if grain were brought under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, then the price of wheat, on the basis of the three years 1943, 1944 and 1945, according to the dominion bureau of statistics would be $2.27 a bushel.
Some people say, well, what would be the reaction of the public if the government maintained support prices at that level? For instance, what would be the attitude of labour? Well, I understand labour has already taken a stand supporting it. I refer to the brief of the interprovincial farm union council, presented to the government on February 16, 1956, and quote from page 13 in reference to this question:
That the consumer would not resist any move that would reimburse farmers on an equitable basis has been proven by the fact that the two main organized labour groups, C.T.L.C. and C.C.L., are on record as being in support of the principle of a fair and equitable price to the primary producer of agricultural products.
No doubt labour realizes it has a very substantial market in the farm industry, and if they hope to be able to sell to the farmers in large volume then the farmers will have to be able to pay for the goods they buy from the secondary industries. In order to do so the farmers will have to receive a price that bears a fair relationship to the prices on other commodities.
The wheat producer is, of course, in worse shape than the majority of farm producers because the price of grain has dropped lower than the price of any other farm commodity. Here again the grain farmers are fully justified in insisting upon an adequate support price today, in view of the fact that they did take a price considerably below the world market price in the years 1945 to 1949.
I have in my hand figures showing the losses that were suffered under the British wheat agreement by comparison with the world market price for class 2 wheat in the years 1946 to 1950, during which period the farmers lost $431,676,844. Then as the result of subsidizing the Canadian consumer at the same price at which we sold wheat to Britain

instead of at the world market price, the farmers lost another $136,920,921. If you add those two figures together you get an over-all total of $568,597,765. If you subtract from that figure $65 million which the government paid to the farmers on account of their losses, you have a net loss of approximately half a billion dollars.
Therefore I do not think any one can argue that the farmers in asking for a support price today are asking for a hand-out. They are merely asking compensation for something they have already paid. They have already paid the premium of half a billion dollars in regard to wheat and many hundreds of millions in regard to prices on other commodities.
I say this in view of the fact that they accepted prices considerably below the world market prices. There are several ways in which support prices may be paid or in which a parity price may be guaranteed. Personally I think the farmers are justified in asking for 100 per cent of parity with the period from 1943 to 1945 for all their produce whether it is sold in Canada or on the external market. On the other hand, however, we recognize that we have no control over the external market, though we do have control over the prices at which commodities are sold in this country.
We in this group have always advocated the adoption of the two-price system. It is interesting to note that the interprovincial farm union has also adopted this policy; that is, a parity price for the production of agricultural products consumed in Canada, and the best price that can be obtained on the world market, preferably through international agreement, for the farm produce sold abroad with a reasonable floor placed under the goods exported abroad.
After all, when you consider that approximately 94 per cent of all farm produce apart from wheat is consumed in Canada, there is no reason why we should allow the 6 per cent that is exported to set the price for the 94 per cent consumed in this country. Therefore we have advocated the two-price system, not because we do not think the farmers are justified in asking for a parity price on all their produce but because it is far easier to put a two-price system into operation. After we have had it in operation, then will be time enough to think about trying to obtain a parity price on the total production.
There are some people who will say that the adoption of a policy which will give the farmers of this country a price for their commodity that will return to them their fair share of the national income will expand the

amount of our surpluses. In that regard I think the time is long overdue for the government to announce a long-term policy. What is the government's policy regarding agricultural production? I think the government should announce to the farmers just what it wants them to do in regard to production. Does the government want the farmers to reduce their production or to maintain it at its present level? If the government wants them to maintain it at the present level, then no one can argue that a policy of price support is to blame for present levels of production, because if the government does not want production to be maintained at present levels it will have to adopt a policy whereby production can be restricted. But just so long as the government does not want production to be restricted there can be no criticism of the farmers' present level of production. When you consider the international situation wherein, according to the FAO, 50 per cent of the population is hungry, I think we can then agree that a policy of maintaining production at a high level is essential at this time.
We in this group have always stated in so far as external markets are concerned that we feel the government should make food available to all those nations who are unable to obtain it through normal channels of trade by such means as acceptance of foreign currency, by barter agreements or in some cases by way of gifts. In so far as the domestic market is concerned, we feel we still have quite a large potential market for increased agricultural production in this country.
The federation of agriculture in its brief suggested a number of means by which we could increase the consumption of dairy products. The federation suggested a free school lunch milk program, a continuation of the policy of making butter available to institutions, and some form of a stamp coupon program in order to get milk and butter to needy people. From time to time we have advocated a similar policy in this house. We have pointed out that a stamp coupon program could be adopted which would be similar to the stamp program carried out in the United States shortly before the war.
It is also interesting to note that the Canadian consumers' association, in a pamphlet they recently put out, also advocated a free school lunch milk program in order to expand the consumption of milk and an expansion of the program of converting milk into milk powder so it can be more easily stored.
If our surpluses continue to rise after the government has done everything conceivably possible to expand our markets for agricultural produce both in the domestic and external fields, I believe the government should 67509-129J
Economic Position of Agriculture then try to build up fairly substantial reserves of all farm commodities that can be stored against the day when crop failures might come. If when we have built up satisfactory reserves surpluses continue, I think the government would be justified in introducing a policy along the lines of the policy it adopted during the war, known as the wheat acreage reduction policy. I would say that policy would only be justified provided they had done everything in their power to expand the domestic and foreign markets and had built up substantial reserves to carry us over for two or three years of crop failures. They might set up something like the soil bank provided by President Eisenhower of the United States to encourage farmers to take poor land out of cultivation and put it into grass or forest. This would help to restore the fertility of the land; and if it were necessary to expand production later on, that land which had been sown to grass and was therefore in a more fertile state could be broken up and put into grain once again.
I submit that the government definitely owes it to the farmers of this country to announce just what they want in that regard. If they want the farmers to continue to expand their production, then they should guarantee that they will not have to suffer a lower price. If on the other hand the government feels that our production of agricultural products today is as high as it is wise to maintain it, the government should announce that and bring in a policy similar to that adopted in the United States in order to encourage farmers to preserve the fertility of their soil.

"it be resolved that the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agricultural and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture and in order that it may receive a just and fair return, and thus be enabled to make that contribution to Canada's war effort which is so desirable, and which our agricultural population so greatly desire to make."
That should make it plain to the C.C.F. party that this was first brought into the

Economic Position of Agriculture House of Commons by the hon. member for Prince Albert back in 1941.

speechtext: Would the hon. member go back to 1931?

speechtext:
I will go back to 1931 in a few minutes if my hon. friend will just wait. I should like now to quote from a speech made by a former leader of this party, John Bracken, at Lethbridge in 1943, when he said:
In order to prevent wide fluctuations of farm prices we shall, in the case of our major export products, provide a floor price below which they will not be permitted to fall, and we shall allow to the producers the benefit of any advance thereon. Since price ceilings are now being maintained to prevent farm prices from rising to high levels in wartime, we shall see to it that price floors are provided, to prevent farm prices from dropping to unfair levels in peacetime. There should not be price ceilings on farm prices to prevent inflation in wartime, without price floors to prevent deflation in peacetime.
Then on March 23, 1953, the hon. member for Prince Albert moved another motion, to be found at page 3208 of Hansard for that year, as follows:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to provide floor prices for agricultural products at such levels as to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship."
Surely that will answer the suggestion made by the hon. member for Assiniboia that this is a new policy on our part. It is not a new policy; we have stood for this policy for 15 years, and we are going to stick with it. As far as the C.C.F. subamendment is concerned we are quite willing to support it.
In regard to the criticism that we did not support the motion moved by the C.C.F. party on May 17, 1954, I think I should reread that motion, which is reported on page 4797 of Hansard and is as follows:
That all the words after the word "That" to the end of the question be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to demonstrating its support of the principle of orderly marketing through livestock marketing boards by announcing floor prices with respect to cattle and hogs at levels not less than the average of the prices which prevailed during the period from January 1, 1951 to December 31. 1953".
This party has never been in favour of a definite stated price for any particular period. We submit that it should be an elastic price. I think probably I should quote the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris to be found on page 4812 of Hansard for that same date. The hon. member said:
As a matter of fact, the present plan has been repudiated by the majority of livestock producer

groups in the province because it is too compulsory and, as has been indicated by the hon. member for Calgary North, it approximates socialized marketing. Among the groups who have not given their support to the plan are the Manitoba pools, which in a largely attended meeting in the city of Brandon just a few weeks ago, while supporting the broad principle of producer marketing boards, opposed to the extent of 90 per cent the proposal that has been put forward by the Manitoba farmers union. Also the Manitoba cattle producers association is opposed to the present plan.
I think we were quite justified in opposing that plan when it had been opposed by so many farm organizations across the country. The hon. member for Mackenzie suggested that I should go back to the 1930's, and I am ready to do that. I am willing to admit that when the Conservative government gave up power in 1935 the prices of agricultural products were low, but I would point out also that after five years of Liberal administration the inequality between the prices of the products the farmer had to buy and the prices of the products he had to sell had grown steadily worse.
In 1935, when the Liberals came into power, the parity prices were 20 per cent below; in 1940, after five years of Liberal administration, they had dropped to 23 per cent below parity. That should answer any question about the 1930's. I will say to the hon. member for Mackenzie that we are almost back now to the same ratio; we are closer to it than we have been at any time since 1932. I have here the Economic Annalist for February, 1956, volume 26, No. 1.
To prove the statement I have just made, I want to give farm prices of agricultural products from 1935 to 1940 on the basis of 100 for the 1935-39 price. In 1935 the figure was 88, in 1936 it was 96-9, in 1937 it was 119-7, in 1938 it was 105, in 1939 it was 91-8 and in 1940 it was 96-8. There was a rise of only 8-8 points in the period from 1935 to 1940. In the case of commodities and services used by farmers and taking the same period of years, 1935 to 1940, there was rise from 95-4 to 106-8, or an increase of 11-4 points. While farm prices fell 8-8 points the commodities the farmers were forced to buy rose 11-4 points.
Then we have the period from 1951 to the present time. On the same basis agricultural products have dropped from 296-8 in 1951 to a figure of 225 -05 for 1955, this figure being the average for the first eleven months of the year. That is a drop of 71-8 points. In the same period commodities and services used by the farmers have risen from 230 to 251-3, or an increase of 21-3 points.
I believe that gives a fairly good idea, Mr. Speaker, of the net position of the farmers of the country today, and after all it is the

net position that actually counts. The Minister of Agriculture can bring all the figures he likes on gross income and net worth statements, but the net income is the only one the farmer knows what it actually means as far as money in his pocket is concerned.

Dollar wheat will give you a job and enable you to own your own home. Dollar wheat will pay for your light and water and give you a telephone. Dollar wheat will pay your grocery bill and buy boots, shoes and clothing for the whole family.

I want to go back again to the brief of the farm union, page 6, where it is definitely stated that 38 per cent of the farmers in this country have a gross income of less than $1,200 a year. This, as I said, is the situation with regard to the farmers' income. While the general economy of Canada has probably never been better, the farmers, one industry, have suffered a 48-22 per cent decline in their income. Practically all others are receiving better incomes than they ever received in their lives before. Is that fair? No one, not even a person on the government side of the house, would state that was a fair situation, or one that could be ignored or about which the government could sit back and take a do nothing attitude.
A Financial Post survey shows that 25 corporations dealing with farmers increased their average profits after taxes by 402 per cent between 1946 and 1954. One of the larger packing companies indicates in its annual report that the average profit over the last 10 years was 27-5 per cent of their capital investment. I would venture to say that there are very few farmers who would not be tickled to death if they could average 2 per cent or 3 per cent net on their capital investment every year.
While some of these companies admit that they buy as cheaply as possible and sell for ss much as possible, most farmers are forced to pay the prices they are asked and to sell for what they are offered. In order to improve their marketing position, many commodity groups have set up plans under provincial marketing legislation to sell their products. Many such plans are in operation in Ontario now, and have been quite successful. Most farmers feel that this method of marketing is one solution to the problem, but certainly it cannot be said that farmers' organizations are not trying to help themselves by every possible avenue open to them.
In view of the fact that the two main labour organizations, the Trades and Labour Congress and the Canadian Congress of Labour, are on record as being in support of the principle of equitable prices to the primary producers of agricultural products, why does this government stubbornly refuse to make adequate use of the existing floor price legislation? We ask, as we have asked on various previous occasions, that the government bring forward an amendment to include in the Agricultural

Prices Support Act a formula which would ensure agriculture producers a fair and equitable basis for arriving at floor prices. The farmers of Canada, comprising approximately 17 per cent of the population in 1954, received 6-8 per cent of the national income. I know quite well, as does everyone else, that the 1955 figure will be still lower. The situation requires a realistic floor price policy for agriculture if the economy of our country is to be maintained at a reasonable level of prosperity.

I simply have to state quite frankly that I am not in a position to answer a question arising out of what happens in the Saskatchewan legislature. I leave it to the members of that legislature to answer for themselves. The question before this house is whether the members of this house who sit on the government side-because they are the ones who are going to decide this issue-are prepared to express their opinions and by a free vote, a free opinion on the merits of the principle in this amendment rather than toeing the party line and voting simply to uphold the government. I hope that before the debate is over the Minister of Agriculture will rise in his place and give freedom to the followers of his party to speak and vote on this question as they please.
Who are the organizations, outside of the membership of this house, who are interested in this issue, and what are their views? I would like to call as the first witness the members of the Manitoba farmers' union in convention in Winnipeg on December 5, 6 and 7, 1955. One of the first resolutions that appeared on the agenda of that convention, which was carried, reads as follows:
Whereas decreased farm income due to depressed prices drastically affects the living standards of the farm family, and
Whereas there appears to be no lessening to any appreciable degree of the price squeeze pressure, and it is quite obvious that the continual deterioration in the agricultural economy is now being reflected to a marked degree in our national economy,
Therefore be it resolved that we urge the federal government to establish a parity price program which will equal 100 per cent of parity on all agricultural products.
That sets out very clearly, without need for much comment, the attitude of the Manitoba farmers' union in convention. I might add that, of course, is also the representative views of the farm unions of all the provinces of Canada.
Then I call as the second witness the presentation made to the Manitoba members of parliament-and that included the federal members of parliament-in December of 1955


by the Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation. In that presentation they had this to say, as shown on page 4 under the heading, "Equality for Agriculture":
We believe that farm families generally, should receive prices or returns that will yield them enough income from farming to maintain a level of living equivalent to that of persons in other occupations with comparable skill, effort and investment.
The M.F.A.C. has, over a long period of time, advocated and worked for equality or parity for agriculture.
That sets out the views of the Manitoba federation of agriculture, which represents a large number of farmers in that province and includes most of the co-operative associations.
We call as a third witness the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which is the parent body of the M.F.A.C., and their annual submission to the government of February 14, 1956. On the fourth page of their brief they had this to say:
Farmers feel that the worsening of their relative position has reached a point where it should be recognized that it Is a vital concern of the public's, as well as of the farmer's, that this trend be halted. The farmer's position is difficult enough now to ensure that he will make any further production adjustments that are within his ability to make. However, it should be emphasized that a continuation of the recent downward trend in farm purchasing power will create economic hardship, make it difficult to maintain adequate municipal and educational services, and delay rather than encourage the further healthy development of agriculture in this country.
That is the studied opinion of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in its submission to the government this year. I think it sets out rather adequately that so far as organized agriculture is concerned, and that includes organized agriculture right across this country, they are in favour of the principle of parity income for agriculture.
We know now that so far as the farmers themselves are concerned they want this to be adopted. So far as hon. members sitting in the opposition are concerned we want this policy adopted, too. That leaves the onus on hon. members sitting on the government side of the house to cast the deciding vote. It is a serious responsibility and one which they cannot take lightly, because this question has reached a point in the thinking of the farm organizations across Canada where I predict it is going to be one of the major issues in the next election.
Hon. members who support the government and who represent agricultural constituencies I think will not be able to wiggle out of that position by simply stating they were voting to uphold this government, as if the government were tottering and ready to fall and

Economic Position of Agriculture
had to be upheld on every occasion. They will have to take the responsibility for their actions as individuals representing the constituencies which they were elected to represent. They will not be able to use as an excuse the fact that the government considered this as a question of want of confidence.
I come now to the second part of what I have to say. I have already discussed who wants parity prices, and I would now like to turn to the question of why we want parity prices for agriculture. It is not only because it is a good subject for academic discussion. It is rather because, from a practical point of view, after having canvassed the situation and the position of agriculture from the various angles, the farm organizations have come to the conclusion that unless this government-or this parliament, to be more exact-takes steps in the near future and takes a hand in the economy of this country with respect to both the income of agriculture and the expenses of agriculture incurred in production, then the downward trend of farm income is going to continue. That situation is aggravated all the more by the fact that while the trend of the returns has been downward, and figures have been quoted today which show that the decrease runs as high as 48 per cent in recent years, the cost of production is still either static or rising.
In a situation of that kind it is not enough for the government to say that it hopes the situation will change because of the trade position, or that markets will increase for other reasons. We have reached the point where we are now either going to take a hand in assisting agriculture to get its share of the national income or we will have to say to agriculture, "We are not going to do anything about it", and the farmers will have to decide as individuals or family units whether they are going to stay in agriculture or do as so many have already done, leave the farms and flock to the cities thereby aggravating the unemployment situation during the slack period, and adding to the problems which already exist in the over-congested cities in our country. Therefore it is a serious question.
I would like to refer to page 5 of the submission made by the interprovincial farm union council to the government on February 16, 1956, in which they point out some of the trends I have been speaking about. We have heard a great deal about the grain situation, but I would like to emphasize the fact that so far as agriculture is concerned,
livestock in my opinion is much more important than grain so far as the stability of income is concerned.
With respect to cattle we find that a comparison between the years 1951 to 1954 shows a steady downward trend. The yearly weighted average price per hundredweight of total sales on public stockyards for cattle in 1951 was $28.22; in 1952, $20.00; in 1953, $15.30; in 1954, $14.45. The statistics do not appear for 1955, but we have no reason to believe that the picture is any better.
We come then to grade A hogs dressed, in the second period 1954-55. In the first half of 1954 the price was $33.33; second half of 1954, $24.92; in the first half of 1955 the price was $23.52; in the second half of 1955, $23.17.
In recent months hon. members of this group have pointed out to the Minister of Agriculture and the government that in many cases the price has dropped even lower than the established price under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
Another interesting set of statistics contained in the same submission is a comparison of the return on investment. There are those who regard agriculture as a business. I personally regard it as something more than that; I think it is a way of life. Let us look at agriculture from the business point of view for the time being. We find as contained on page 8 of this submission that in 1954 Canada Packers Limited showed a return on capital investment of 25-2 per cent whereas in the same year, if you take the grouping of all farmers in the province of Manitoba and take into consideration their investment and return, in 1954 their return on investment amounted to -001 per cent. That is a very striking contrast as to what the returns on investment are for agriculture as compared with another industry.
Figures have been given today to show the comparative share of the national income or the gross national product received by farmers as compared with the national economy generally. We find that in 1952 farmers received 11-4 per cent of the national income, whereas on a proportionate basis they should have received something like 20 per cent. In 1953 they received 9-9 per cent. In 1954 it went down to 6-8 per cent, and no doubt it will be less than that in 1955, probably around 6 per cent. There again we have plenty of evidence to show that on that basis agriculture has good reason for asking that this parliament take action with respecl to a parity income for agriculture in order tc ensure that farmers get something like theii fair share of the national income.
I come now to the third heading, and tha'
is how can we establish parity income foi

Economic Position of Agriculture agriculture. I said earlier that the methods may differ. Other hon. members may have their own ideas as to how this can be done, and I for one will be very glad to hear them. The government itself may have some ideas on this question, but in my own opinion and speaking for myself I think there are two main channels through which we can approach the question of parity income for agriculture.
One of these would be a method of setting a system of floor prices and using subsidies where necessary to maintain those floor prices. Under that system it would be necessary to extend the provisions of the Agricultural Prices Support Act in order to make greater use of marketing boards, because it is only through a system of marketing boards that this act can be properly administered, as I shall show in a minute or two. Wherever it is found necessary, in order to maintain floor prices as a protection or guarantee against a fire sale of a particular product, this parliament should be prepared to vote moneys to be used as subsidies to uphold those floor prices.
I should like to mention this because when hon. members in this house speak about subsidies in order to maintain floor prices, there are many people in the country who do not quite understand what is involved. They have a vision of this parliament having to vote hundreds of millions of dollars annually for the purpose of subsidizing this, that or some other agricultural product. If we have a system of guaranteed floor prices that is not necessarily what is going to happen, and I am fairly sure that is not what would happen.
There would be times when this parliament would be called upon to make an appropriation in order to prevent the surplus of a certain product depressing the price of the whole market at that point, but as long as the market price remained at the level of the floor price or higher it would not cost the public treasury one cent in the form of subsidy to maintain the floor price. That is something that should be emphasized and understood, that a floor price and the willingness to maintain a floor price by means of a subsidy does not necessarily involve the expenditure of public money. It acts as insurance; this government could act as an underwriter in order to prevent prices falling below a certain floor. We should be prepared to use public funds to maintain that floor price.
There is another method which I believe could be used alongside this one, but which is not being used at the present time, and I refer to price control. I remember during


last session we were told a number of times that one of the reasons we cannot expect farmers to get better prices for certain products was the necessity of meeting world competition. We were told that therefore they had to keep their prices at a level which would be competitive with the prices of agricultural products elsewhere. They were advised from time to time to cut down their cost of production by greater efficiency, by the use of more modern methods, by greater production per unit and in that way be able to compete on the world markets.
We know that the possibility of their doing that is limited strictly by the factors which enter into the cost of production. If we are going to accept the principle or the idea or the theory that we should try to produce agricultural products at prices which will be competitive with agricultural products grown in other countries, then we will have to take steps to see that the cost of the articles which the farmer has to buy and which enter into his cost of production are controlled.
I think that in order to have a really successful system of parity prices in this country we shall have to employ eventually both these methods or a combination of them, that is a system of floor prices with marketing boards for their administration and a system of price control in order to maintain the cost of production at a reasonable figure. If the cost of production is not controlled we may find that many of the advantages of floor prices would be frittered away by those who are in position to exploit the farmer through profiteering.
In my opinion the whole question boils down to providing sufficient purchasing power within our own country to make it possible for the people to buy at the proper price level all the agricultural products required by our population, and having some machinery set up for the purpose of assisting in the sale of our surplus products on the world market, not at the cost of the producer but if necessary at the cost of the nation as a whole.
I want to emphasize again that the most important and most desirable market for agricultural products that can be found anywhere in the world is the market we have right here in Canada. There are hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions of people who would be using more food, a better quality of food and in greater quantities if they had sufficient income to be able to do so.
This was illustrated most vividly during the years of the war and immediately after the war. When money began to circulate in this country and people began to have steadier jobs at better pay we found that the consumption of agricultural products began to rise so

markedly that during the war years we had to have food rationing because the demand was beginning to exceed the supply. Now the shoe seems to be on the other foot. If we could do something, if we could increase the purchasing power of the Canadian people and bring about that happy relationship where effective demand would more or less equal supply, then we would have an ideal situation.
I should like to finish before six o'clock, and if I could take just one minute I should like to set before the house five points which I believe should be followed in order to bring about this sufficient effective purchasing power to provide a better market for agricultural products in our own country.
First, we should accept the principle of parity for agriculture.
Second, I would advocate a system of floor prices to be established for producers. I emphasize floor prices for producers, because under the Agricultural Prices Support Act we find that even where floor prices are established they work to the advantage of the packers or dealers and do not find their way down to the producer level.
Third, the establishment of low cost credit for our agricultural producer.
Fourth, effective action to prevent monopolies and combines. I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand say that an industry which does business with the farmers had increased its profits by something like 402 per cent. I think I heard the hon. member correctly, and if he confirms that figure there is something wrong when we find that the income of agriculture has dropped by 48 per cent in recent years while the profits of this industry which deals with the agricultural industry have increased by 402 per cent. They do not do that by ordinary business practices. We know that monopolies and combines constitute a greater danger and threat to our economy than ever before, and effective steps should be taken to combat that type of practice.
Fifth, and perhaps as important as any of the others, is the fact that if we are to have sufficient effective purchasing power in this country we must expand to the greatest possible extent our social welfare legislation to provide all those who need goods and can use them with the purchasing power in order that they can buy the good things of life that we have in such abundance in this country.

Mr. Speaker, the matter before the house is perhaps one of the most important and challenging that has ever come before this assembly. We are now discussing the matter of asking the government to give consideration to bringing in a policy of parity prices for agriculture. I say this, Mr. Speaker, because unless we can bring about for agriculture policies which will give a fair share of the national income to our agricultural producers I think we shall have difficulty in every part of our economy.
Before the dinner recess I was most interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Dauphin, when he stated he believed that if members on the government side of the house were given the liberty of voting according to their feelings with respect to this matter, and if a free vote were allowed, they would join with members on the opposition benches in supporting this resolution.

I think there are three phases in respect of this whole problem; first, the economic position of agriculture; second, what does the future hold for agriculture; and third, how can we achieve our objective? There may be some people who are not too greatly concerned about agriculture. They think perhaps the Canadian economy, with its buoyancy in the industrial field today, is sufficient to sustain a relatively high income for our Canadian people. On the other hand I am sure that agriculture will be in the future, as it has been in the past, the chief segment of our economy upon which we can build the strength of our prosperity. For this reason I think we should examine all phases of the economic position of agriculture at the present time.
It is true that we have many sources of information coming to various members of the house in respect of farm income, both on a national and a regional basis. While it is true that the general Canadian economic picture is not so bad-the figure is just down a few points; 3 per cent or a little less when one considers the whole of the Canadian economy -on the other hand in western Canada we have a situation where the three western provinces during these last three years have experienced a tragic drop in farm income. According to the Canadian Wheat Pool of February 6, 1956, the total farm income for 1954 was $2,377 million, or $398 million below

Economic Position of Agriculture that of 1953. It is also a very important matter that the income of the farmers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta'-that is, their 1954 income-was down a total of $404 million, some 28 per cent below the 1953 income.
It is true that during this period profits and in many industries wages boomed. But we have the three western provinces with their income down 28 per cent from 1953. As I stated earlier, we have a number of sources from which we can find out the kind of income which farmers are receiving today. While newspapers across the country have expressed concern with respect to farm income, I think this government has not yet awakened to the seriousness of the situation. I have here a clipping from the Montreal Gazette of January 18, 1956 in respect of farm income. The Bank of Nova Scotia monthly review has this to say:
The continued restriction of farm purchasing power in the west and the failure of the farm sector generally to share in the buoyancy that characterized other parts of the economy in 1955 cannot be regarded lightly . . .
Then it goes on to point out the drop in income. Again, the Windsor Star of January 12, 1956, contains an article quoting the words of Professor Buckley, who states that although the prairie people are aware of the fact, he thinks the rest of Canada is not impressed with the reality. Then again the Ottawa Citizen of December 22 had this to say, quoting H. H. Hannam. The article states that farm income has dropped 23 per cent from 1951, and then Mr. Hannam says:
How would anyone else like to take a 25 per cent salary cut?
And he goes on to say this:
We are not hollering blue ruin or depression, but now is the time when the downward trend must be checked.

Again, Mr. Speaker, the Globe and Mail of February 17, 1956, contains an article under the heading "Low Incomes driving Farmers from Land". While it indicates again the drop in farm income it has this to say:
Canada Packers Limited shows an indicated average profit for 10 years of 27.5 per cent on their capital investment. This is more than three times the expected return on general investments and 25 times more than was received by farmers on their capital investment in 1954.
As I said before, it seems difficult to convince this government that we need for Canada agricultural policies to prevent this sort of downward spiralling of farm prices. In that connection the Winnipeg Free Press of December 29, 1955 has this to say. The article is headed "The West ignored". Commenting in the report of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on economic conditions in Canada, it says:
Mr, Howe's review has one other feature of note, and particularly of note to western Canada. The review largely ignores western Canada. It describes the economy in a state of vigorous expansion, bordering on the dangers of speculative excesses and an inflationary boom. This is entirely accurate for most sections of the economy. It is not the whole picture for the prairies. It ignores the state of the farmer.
I fear that is the important point in the discussion which is taking place at this time, Mr. Speaker, and indeed in relation to the arguments and discussions which have taken place since this new session began. From coast to coast the state of agriculture is a fiasco, and this government has not seen fit to do much about it. As I stated before, I think we must examine the economic position of the farmer. I have given some excerpts from newspaper thought in respect of the question, and I should now like to examine it a little more closely.
I have here a chart prepared by the dominion bureau of statistics dated February 26, 1956. This chart shows farm income, farm expenses and value of farm capital in Canada from 1945 to 1954. It shows the gross income, operating costs, depreciation, net income and value of farm capital. I am just going to illustrate the situation in 1951. There was a gross income of $3,578 million; operating costs were $1,238 million; depreciation, $196 million; net income, $2,154 million.
The important thing, Mr. Speaker is this. By 1954 the gross income had dropped to $2,624 million; operating costs had risen to $1,255 million; depreciation was even higher, $245 million. The net income had again dropped from a high in 1951 of $2,154 million to $1,125 million. This chart illustrates and gives a vivid graphic picture of farm

income in Canada. Rather than try to put the whole thing on the record, I should like the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, to place this chart on Hansard.

I should like also to illustrate the purchasing power of the farmer's dollar in 1954 in relation to other years. Again I am not going to use too many figures. We can go back to 1910 and see that the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat was $1.29. In 1954-55 with the initial price at $1.40, the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat had decreased to 61-4 cents. I submit I have put sufficient figures on the record to indicate the plight of agriculture today.
Now, I think we should try to examine the future. I am most impressed with the fact that it was the Conservative party which this afternoon moved for parity prices. I feel we have long since convinced many people in Canada that unless agriculture gets a fair share of the national income, unless we have agriculture policies in this country which will give the farmer a fair relationship between the things he has to sell and the things he has to buy, we cannot have justice and certainly we cannot have a stable economy.
This government may not worry very much about what is happening in agriculture. I, for one, want to join with those people who believe that the family farm is the type of farm we should support in making our policies. I believe policies of that type will add strength to the family and to our nation generally. I am going to suggest to this government that unless they can take this
problem in hand and see to it that the family farm is saved from disintegration, we are going to have bigger and bigger farms in this country. This has been the trend in the United States for many years, and perhaps it still is. We see this happening in Canada today. The investment necessary to start a small farm today is too large for the young farmer to undertake. I noticed that in the submission the Manitoba government made to the Gordon commission they indicated that $17,000 was the capital investment in the average Manitoba farm. I believe it would be somewhat higher in Saskatchewan. It is clear that a young man wanting to take up agriculture as his way of life is not likely to be able to finance the undertaking.
We do not have a national policy on credit that would give low interest loans and enable a young man to set himself up on the farm. Indeed, today under the various acts providing for farm loans and farm improvement loans, the interest rate is quite a bit too high. Young people graduating from high school or university who would like to go on farms are forced to find other occupations just because proper financing is not available to enable them to undertake agriculture.
In addition to that there are the fluctuations and vagaries of this system, not the law of supply and demand, but purely the fact that the individual farmer gets little help and is

Economic Position of Agriculture expected to market his products under conditions over which he has no control.
I want, therefore, to support the principle of parity prices. As I said before, the interprovincial farm union council and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture support parity prices. We have, too, the large labour unions in this country supporting the principle of fairness and equity for agriculture.
I have here a clipping from the Globe and Mail of February 20 which I should like to read. It says:
T.L.C. chief, Claude Jodoin and C.C.L. head A. R. Mosher-whose organizations are soon to amalgamate-agreed also that farmers should get "equitable" or parity prices on all farm products.
In respect to this whole argument on parity prices, there are those who say they are in favour of agriculture getting a fair share of the national income but they are against parity prices. I do not know how you can have it both ways. I do not know how you can say you are prepared to support policies which will guarantee the producers a fair share of the national income, yet at the same time you are against parity prices. I find it difficult to see how such people can be sincere. I feel that the two are synonymous. Parity prices simply mean justice and equity for the agriculture producer.
I do not believe it does much good to go into the past. I think we should be looking to the future. I feel sure the Minister of Agriculture would join the rest of us if he were a free agent and able to state whether or not he was in favour of parity for agriculture. I would suggest that members on the Liberal benches who come from the prairie provinces and represent agricultural constituencies should get up and state what they think about this. I agree with the hon. member for Dauphin. When the federal election rolls around I do not believe any western farmer will believe any of those hon. members who say, "Oh, yes, we are in favour of it; we are in favour of parity prices, but we could not do anything else because we had to support the government." Everyone in Canada knows that this government has such a preponderance of numbers on the benches opposite that they could send 100 members home and still carry measures; there would be little chance of the government being defeated. Of course, at times they are not all in the house. If the government wanted to, it could have a free vote. They could take off the whips and let hon. members rise to their feet and say what they believe.
Since I am talking about farm income, may I say that I have heard the Minister of Agriculture out west state his financial position as a farmer. I do not want to be unfair

about this; but he knows full well the vagaries of agriculture, of nature, and the fluctuations in prices with which the farmer has to cope. He knows that for many years as a farmer he himself was in the position that many farmers in western Canada are facing today. If he would try to get his colleagues to say that in the interests of every Canadian we have to do something tangible in order to meet the challenge before us-[DOT]

speechtext:
Now
you have a big majority, but that is no reason for doing what you like. More than that, if you were in favour of this resolution you would have the support of all the members on the opposition benches. Therefore I do not think your argument holds water at all.
What we are asking for, Mr. Speaker, is a national policy adequate to meet the need. First, we should have a low interest rate so that any young farmer in Canada could go into agriculture as his life work, as his vocation. Second, and this is most important, we should have a policy which would give stability to the various kinds of production. At the present time there is pressure on the marketing of hogs and cattle. I believe it was just two years ago that the Minister of Agriculture suggested to western farmers that if they wanted to get ready cash they should feed some of their grain.
I notice he is not advocating that today. Why not? He knows that today there is pressure on the hog market and the beef market, and that perhaps prices will collapse. Already the hog market is so depressed that many farmers are receiving returns for their hogs below what is supposed to be the support price. The whole agricultural economic picture is in a state of chaos; it is a fiasco, and this government is not prepared to do anything about it.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that those who say higher prices for agricultural products will only mean that the consumers will pay higher prices are not correct. Fair prices, adequate prices, which mean parity to the farmer, do not mean higher prices to the consumer. May I give one specific example in respect of wheat. I have taken the trouble to make some investigations, and I find that one bushel of the higher milling grades of wheat will produce about 72-2 per cent of flour. At the

present prices for top grade wheat the farmer will get anywhere from 96 cents to $1.25 per bushel for that wheat. He will receive 1J to 2i cents a pound. As soon as that wheat is made into flour the price increases to 5| cents a pound, and when it is made into bread it retails at 15 cents a pound. One hundred pounds of flour will make 129 loaves of bread, and at present prices they will retail at around $8.66.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the house can see what happens. The farmer produces the wheat, but the price he receives for that wheat has very little to do with the price the consumer pays for a loaf of bread. That is also true of canned vegetables and many other things which the farmers produce. Therefore it is not a fact that fair prices to the producer would mean higher prices to the consumer.
As I said in the early part of my remarks, the people who are handling the farmers' products, such as the packers, are receiving tremendous profits, but the farmer himself is in a depressed state. What I am suggesting, Mr. Speaker, is that the time is ripe for this government to take adequate action to underwrite a comprehensive parity price policy for all of Canada.
We have far too much urbanization in this country. Far too many people are leaving the farms, not because they could not be made economic, not because farmers are not using new techniques, or are not attempting to be as scientific in their production as any other business. They are leaving the farms because of the marketing and price situation over which they have little or no control. I am suggesting that the only authoritative body that is given the power by the people of this country is the federal government. Unless they are ready to take action, agriculture in this country will face a very blue future.
Many other countries are awakening to the fact that they must have adequate agricultural prices to meet the challenge of the day. In this country we should have policies under which we would conserve the nutritive content of the soil. We should have a policy under which a farmer could buy fertilizer and add it to the soil so that future generations would be assured of high fertility in our soil. We should have a conservation program under which a farmer could undertake those projects necessary to prevent the erosion of the soil. We have just a hit and miss policy. Under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act some money has been expended, but up to the present time we have not a comprehensive national system for agriculture which meets the challenge of
Economic Position of Agriculture the day. Here is one place where we should make a beginning and establish parity prices for agriculture.
I agree with the hon. member for Dauphin. It would not necessarily mean, if such a policy were established, that we would be paying money out of the federal treasury to support the principle. Only in those times when due to outside influences the market is depressed, would it be necessary for the federal government to step in and use money from the federal treasury to guarantee a fair price to the producer which would bear some relation to the cost of production.
We have seen the prices of things which the farmer grows going down and down into the cellar, and the cost of his production going up and up. We have seen the cost of machinery and the cost of fuel and the cost of everything that goes into his production going up and up. We find that machine companies who hold either a monopoly or a semimonopoly in that field are able to demand from the farmer the price he will pay for those goods. As a matter of fact, we all know that when the farmer goes to sell his goods he asks, "How much will you give me for this?" When he goes to buy he asks, "How much do you want for this?" Unless this government is prepared to step in and give a fair deal to agriculture we shall continue to have a depressed industry.
Therefore I hope that when the time comes to vote on this motion the government, perhaps through the Minister of Agriculture, will rise and say to the house that all members are to be allowed a free vote. I think it would be refreshing if at this time hon. members who come from the west, were to rise and state the real condition of agriculture. Many of them did not do so during the debate on the farm loans bill, but I think that now this important measure is before us hon. members could, to some extent at least, say what they think concerning this important matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment now before the house has to do with the problem of agriculture, certainly the most urgent and complex problem of all those facing our economy at this time. It requires immediate action on the part of the government.
The problem of wheat surpluses in western Canada has provided grounds for extended discussions since the beginning of this session. I will therefore not labour the point.

Economic Position of Agriculture
The two bills which the government has put through, and which involve an expenditure of 30 million dollars to be borne by the taxpayers of this country are sufficiently indicative to the economic status of the western farmer at this time.
While I do not wish to minimize the importance of this matter of wheat surpluses, which is such as to exert a considerable influence on our national revenue, it is certain that the personal problems of each and every farmer in Quebec, taken individually, are just as critical, if not more so.
Mr. Speaker, farm income has decreased by 5 or 10 per cent in 1955 and probably even more in areas where, for instance, hog-raising is practised. In short, it means that since 1952, i.e. for the past three years, the net farm income has decreased by 50 per cent.
After three consecutive years of set-backs, farmers have drained their savings from the years of prosperity and are now penniless; their problem is similar to that of western farmers.
Today, farmers of the province of Quebec have to keep up their farm either by mortgaging their property or by further increasing their debt to the bank, the credit union, their suppliers, merchants, and so on, instead of deriving from their farm an income that will provide them with a decent standard of living.
We hear everywhere that Canada has just had the best year in all her history. Our national income has exceeded $26 billion, and forecasts for 1956 are most optimistic. Company balance sheets show record profits. Individual income has jumped in a similar proportion. Our export and import trade reaches record figures. Production has never been so high.
On the labour front, 1955 has meant another step forward for our labour force, in that they got a guaranteed annual wage from certain industries, and everywhere the renewal of contracts under collective bargaining shows salary increases and additional fringe benefits. The government has even increased unemployment insurance benefits. In short, Mr. Speaker, living conditions seem to be getting better everywhere in this country which is going through an extraordinary development.
This is true of industry, trade and various other sectors of our economy, but it seems that in this development, agriculture has not been able to hold its own and, instead of benefiting from this general prosperity, the farmer is going through a period of depression.
TMr. Perron.]

This, to my mind, sums up the present position. It is an alarming one. It is certainly the crucial issue at this time and it is up to the government to straighten out, by appropriate means, the economic disparity between some otherwise comparable professional groups.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) is, I think, well suited to restore the balance in this field.
The government has explained the policy it means to follow to improve the lot of the western farmer; but we have as yet not been told of its intentions with regard to the eastern farmer. There was no reference to it in the speech from the throne, and for the past two months not a single word has been uttered about it by the government. When the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made his statement about the estimates of his department, apart from burying us under a stack of statistics designed to prove that everything is all right-which merely shows that anything can be made out of statistics-had nothing to say about any steps the government meant to take in order to bring relief to the eastern farmer.
No problem can be solved by avoiding reference to it, or by quoting statistics to show that all goes well, when everyone agrees that things are pretty bad despite anything that may be said by all the economists and statisticians in the world.
One of the questions of particular concern to eastern farmers, since it is vital to them, is to know whether or not the government will continue its price support policy. I hope that the house will be told about this during the present debate, as this would be in perfect agreement with the amendment now before us.
It is absolutely essential that the support price of butter be maintained at 58 cents per pound for the present year and even for two years. The farmer would then know beforehand where he is going. It would alleviate his worries and the uncertainty which always confronts him. Everyone agrees that in the province of Quebec the dairy industry is the basis of agriculture. It is the one that must be saved first. There is no reason why the support price should not be kept this year at the same level since the cost of production has remained exactly the same and because, since 1949, that legislation has cost very little to Canadian taxpayers while it has, on the other hand, protected the consumer by avoiding

those price variations which are often so costly for him.
If the government does not maintain the same level, the farmers of the province of Quebec who will thus be deprived of their one and only sure source of revenue will be ruined.
I therefore urge the government to come to an immediate decision and to tell the house about it without delay.
Mr. Speaker, I stated at the outset that farm income has dropped from 5 to 10 per cent in 1955 mainly because the price of hogs, which remained at 23 cents a pound, the support price set by the government, for several months, has dropped considerably. This, in turn, brought about a decline of farm income in the district of Quebec, particularly in my riding and in the surrounding counties where hog-breeding is practised on a large scale. In fact, the price of feeds and breeding costs remained stationary while the price of pork which, last year, was 27, 28 and 29 cents a pound, was reduced by 5, 6 and even 7 cents a pound, thus depriving the farmer of the profits which he could reap from this operation.
The only way to correct this situation would seem to be an increase of 3 cents in the support price of hogs, to give the farmer a chance to make ends meet.
In connection with hog raising it must not be forgotten that it is at the government's request that farmers, during the war, invested their money in piggeries so as to obtain a new source of revenue. Nowadays, in a great many cases, this operation is no longer profitable. The only way in which it may be made so again would be an increase in the support price to 26 cents a pound.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Prince Albert is such as to solve the farm problem. In fact, I will go so far as to say that it is the one and only solution to this problem.
To sum up, I would say that this amendment should be unanimously carried by the house. I feel too that the government should follow this up by adopting the following two measures.
1.	Maintenance of the support price of butter at 58 cents a pound, and
2.	An increase in the support price of pork from 23 to 26 cents a pound.
Mr. Speaker, the constitutional responsibility of the federal government is to solve these farm problems, and the farmer is rightfully entitled to this solution.
